name: Halothane
description: {"atc": "N01AB01", "indications": "Induction and maintenance of general anesthesia; historical agent of choice for pediatric mask induction where sevoflurane is unavailable. Included in WHO Model List of Essential Medicines.", "mechanism": "Positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A and glycine receptors, inhibition of NMDA and neuronal nicotinic receptors, and hyperpolarization of CNS neuronal membranes via two-pore domain potassium channels (TREK).", "pharmacokinetics": "Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) ~0.75% (high potency); Blood-gas partition coefficient 2.4 (moderate induction/emergence speed); Hepatic metabolism ~15-20% via CYP2E1 to trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) intermediates; excreted by lungs.", "pearls": "⚠️ Halothane Hepatitis: Immune-mediated fulminant hepatic necrosis triggered by TFA-protein neoantigens. Repeated exposure within 3 months significantly increases risk. ⚠️ Malignant Hyperthermia (MH) trigger: Mutated RYR1 receptor causes uncontrolled sarcoplasmic calcium release; treat with IV Dantrolene (2.5 mg/kg bolus). Sensitizes myocardium to arrhythmogenic effects of circulating catecholamines (adrenaline).", "contraindications": "History of unexplained jaundice or pyrexia after previous halogenated anesthetic exposure. Personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia. Severe preexisting hepatic impairment.", "dosageForms": "Volatile liquid for inhalation: 250 mL amber glass bottles (requires calibrated Halothane vaporizer).", "monitoring": "Continuous core body temperature (hyperthermia watch), end-tidal halothane concentration (EtHal), continuous ECG (arrhythmia detection), capnography (EtCO2), and non-invasive blood pressure."}

name: Isoflurane
description: {"atc": "N01AB06", "indications": "Maintenance of general anesthesia in adults and children; neurosurgical anesthesia due to cerebral protection and reduction of cerebral metabolic rate (CMRO2); ICU sedation via specialized delivery devices. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Enhances inhibitory GABA-A and glycine-mediated transmission; inhibits excitatory central synaptic transmission. Reduces cerebral metabolic oxygen consumption while preserving intracranial pressure autoregulation at <1 MAC.", "pharmacokinetics": "MAC 1.15%; Blood-gas partition coefficient 1.4 (faster emergence than halothane); <0.2% hepatic metabolism (negligible hepatic toxicity risk); exhaled unchanged via pulmonary ventilation.", "pearls": "Pungent, ethereal odor causes coughing, breath-holding, and laryngospasm during mask induction (unsuitable for inhalational induction without prior IV induction). Potent systemic vasodilator causing dose-dependent decrease in blood pressure with preserved cardiac output. Theoretical risk of 'coronary steal' in ischemic heart disease, but clinically benign in practice.", "contraindications": "Susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia. Known hypersensitivity to halogenated anesthetics.", "dosageForms": "Volatile liquid for inhalation: 100 mL and 250 mL bottles for Isoflurane-specific vaporizers.", "monitoring": "End-tidal agent monitoring (EtIso), continuous pulse oximetry, capnography, core temperature, blood pressure."}

name: Sevoflurane
description: {"atc": "N01AB08", "indications": "Inhalational induction and maintenance of general anesthesia for adult, pediatric, and ambulatory day-case surgical procedures. The global standard for smooth pediatric mask induction. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptor chloride channels causing CNS hyperpolarization and hypnosis. Rapidly depresses cortical and thalamic neuronal discharge.", "pharmacokinetics": "MAC 2.05% (age-dependent; higher in neonates ~3.3%); Blood-gas partition coefficient 0.65 (very low solubility, yielding ultra-rapid induction and rapid emergence); Hepatic metabolism ~3-5% via CYP2E1 generating inorganic fluoride.", "pearls": "Pleasant, non-pungent, sweet odor makes it the gold-standard agent for gas induction in pediatrics and patients with difficult airways. High risk of emergence delirium in pediatric patients (treat with low-dose propofol, fentanyl, or dexmedetomidine). Reacts with dry barium hydroxide lime or soda lime CO2 absorbents to produce 'Compound A' (nephrotoxic in rats; clinical significance minimal if fresh gas flow >= 1 L/min).", "contraindications": "Known or suspected genetic susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia. Prior severe hepatic dysfunction following halogenated anesthetics.", "dosageForms": "Inhalational liquid: 250 mL bottles with Quik-Fil or standard pour-fill adapter.", "monitoring": "Continuous capnography, end-tidal sevoflurane concentration, train-of-four (TOF) monitoring for neuromuscular synergy, core temperature, ECG."}

name: Desflurane
description: {"atc": "N01AB07", "indications": "Maintenance of general anesthesia in adults, particularly bariatric, lengthy, and elderly procedures requiring rapid, predictable emergence and airway reflex recovery.", "mechanism": "Positive modulation of GABA-A and glycine receptors, inhibition of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the central nervous system.", "pharmacokinetics": "MAC 6.0%; Blood-gas partition coefficient 0.42 (lowest solubility of all volatile agents, closest to nitrous oxide); Hepatic metabolism <0.02% (essentially zero); Boiling point 23.5°C requiring electrically heated, pressurized vaporizers (Tec 6).", "pearls": "Extremely low blood solubility provides instantaneous titratability and ultra-rapid cognitive recovery even after 6+ hours of surgery. Highly pungent and irritant to the airway mucosa: rapid concentration increase triggers sympathetic surge (tachycardia, hypertension), coughing, and bronchospasm (never use for inhalational induction). High global warming potential (~2,500x CO2).", "contraindications": "Susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia; severe reactive airway disease/bronchial asthma for induction; pediatric induction.", "dosageForms": "Volatile liquid for inhalation: 240 mL bottles for heated pressurized vaporizers.", "monitoring": "Continuous end-tidal agent tracking, arterial line/NIBP, heart rate, capnography, depth of anesthesia (BIS/Entropy)."}

name: Nitrous oxide
description: {"atc": "N01AX63", "indications": "Adjunct to general inhalational anesthesia for maintenance of analgesia; labor analgesia (Entonox: 50% N2O / 50% O2); procedural sedation for minor trauma and dental procedures. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist (analgesic effect); stimulates endogenous opioid peptide release in periaqueductal gray; weak GABA-A receptor facilitation.", "pharmacokinetics": "MAC 104% (cannot produce surgical anesthesia alone under normobaric conditions); Blood-gas partition coefficient 0.47 (rapid onset and offset); 'Second gas effect' accelerates uptake of co-administered volatile anesthetics.", "pearls": "Diffuses 34x faster into air-filled closed body cavities than nitrogen leaves them: strictly contraindicated in pneumothorax, bowel obstruction, air embolism, middle ear surgery, and post-vitrectomy retinal gas bubbles. Oxidizes cobalt in vitamin B12, irreversibly inhibiting methionine synthase (risk of megaloblastic anemia, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord with chronic abuse or MTHFR deficiency). Diffusion hypoxia at end of case requires 100% O2 for 5 minutes.", "contraindications": "Pneumothorax, decompression sickness, intestinal obstruction, recent eye surgery with intraocular gas, head injury with impaired consciousness, severe pulmonary hypertension.", "dosageForms": "Medical gas cylinder (blue cylinder, liquid-gas equilibrium at 50 bar) or premixed with oxygen (50:50 Entonox).", "monitoring": "Fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2 > 30% always to avoid hypoxic gas mixture), pulse oximetry, continuous capnography."}

name: Thiopental
description: {"atc": "N01AF03", "indications": "Intravenous rapid-sequence induction of general anesthesia; refractory status epilepticus; reduction of intracranial pressure (ICP) in severe traumatic brain injury. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Ultra-short-acting barbiturate that binds GABA-A receptors, prolonging chloride channel opening duration. Suppresses cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2) and cerebral blood flow (CBF).", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset <30 seconds ('arm-to-brain circulation time'); Duration of hypnosis 5-10 minutes due to rapid redistribution from brain to skeletal muscle and fat; Elimination half-life 11.5 hours (zero-order kinetics at high doses, hepatic accumulation).", "pearls": "Intra-arterial injection causes severe vasospasm, thrombosis, and gangrene of the extremity (immediate management: leave cannula in situ, inject heparin, procaine/lidocaine, and consider brachial plexus block). Venodilator and myocardial depressant: causes profound hypotension in hypovolemic patients. ⚠️ Absolutely contraindicated in acute intermittent porphyria (induces ALA synthase).", "contraindications": "Porphyria (variegate, acute intermittent); severe cardiovascular collapse; status asthmaticus (does not blunt airway reflexes; histamine release).", "dosageForms": "Powder for injection: 500 mg and 1 g vials reconstituted with sterile water to 2.5% solution (pH 10.5, highly alkaline).", "monitoring": "Continuous invasive/non-invasive blood pressure, continuous ECG, airway patency, neurologic examination, cerebral perfusion pressure."}

name: Propofol
description: {"atc": "N01AX10", "indications": "Induction and maintenance of general anesthesia (TIVA - Total Intravenous Anesthesia); procedural sedation (endoscopy, cardioversion); ICU sedation in mechanically ventilated adults. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors, directly activates beta subunit chloride channels at high concentrations; inhibits NMDA receptors and reduces presynaptic glutamate release.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset 30-45 seconds; Duration 5-10 minutes (redistribution); Clearance 1.5-2.2 L/min (exceeds hepatic blood flow, indicating extrahepatic/pulmonary metabolism); Glucuronide conjugation in liver; Context-sensitive half-time remains short (<40 min for infusions up to 8 hrs).", "pearls": "Potent antiemetic properties via 5-HT3 antagonism and chemoreceptor trigger zone suppression (first choice for patients with history of PONV). Pain on IV injection in ~70% of patients (prevent with pre-treatment IV Lidocaine 20-40 mg or large antecubital vein). Vasodilator with blunted baroreceptor reflex causing significant drop in MAP. ⚠️ Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS): Rare but fatal complication with prolonged high-dose infusions (>4 mg/kg/hr for >48 hrs): severe metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis, hepatomegaly, and refractory cardiogenic shock.", "contraindications": "Hypersensitivity to soybean oil, glycerol, or egg lecithin (emulsion vehicle). Severe hemodynamic instability without prior resuscitation. Pediatric ICU sedation for >24 hours.", "dosageForms": "Lipid emulsion for IV injection/infusion: 1% (10 mg/mL) and 2% (20 mg/mL) in 20 mL, 50 mL, and 100 mL vials.", "monitoring": "Continuous blood pressure, ECG, SpO2, depth of anesthesia (Processed EEG / BIS 40-60 during TIVA), serum triglycerides and arterial blood gas if infusing >24 hrs."}

name: Etomidate
description: {"atc": "N01AX07", "indications": "Induction of general anesthesia in patients with severe cardiac disease, hypovolemia, cardiogenic shock, or severe hemodynamic compromise.", "mechanism": "Potent GABA-A receptor modulator binding the beta subunit to enhance GABA-mediated chloride conductance. Zero intrinsic alpha- or beta-adrenergic receptor activity.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset 30-60 seconds; Duration 3-5 minutes (rapid redistribution); High protein binding (75%); Hepatic ester hydrolysis to inactive carboxylic acid metabolite; Clearance 18-25 mL/kg/min.", "pearls": "Exceptional hemodynamic stability: minimal to no change in myocardial contractility, heart rate, systemic vascular resistance, or blood pressure. Decreases cerebral metabolic rate (CMRO2) and intracranial pressure. High incidence of myoclonus upon induction (~30-60%, blunted by opioid pre-treatment). ⚠️ Adrenocortical suppression: Reversibly inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, blocking conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol for up to 24-48 hours after a single bolus dose (use with caution in septic shock). High incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV).", "contraindications": "Known hypersensitivity to etomidate or propylene glycol vehicle; severe primary adrenocortical insufficiency.", "dosageForms": "IV injectable solution: 2 mg/mL in 10 mL and 20 mL ampoules (formulated with 35% propylene glycol or lipid emulsion).", "monitoring": "ECG, continuous blood pressure, clinical monitoring for signs of adrenal insufficiency in critical illness, PONV prophylaxis."}

name: Ketamine
description: {"atc": "N01AX03", "indications": "Induction and maintenance of anesthesia in hemodynamically unstable/shock patients and severe bronchospasm; procedural sedation in emergency and pediatric medicine; subanesthetic infusion for refractory acute/postoperative pain and treatment-resistant depression. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Non-competitive antagonist of phencyclidine site on NMDA receptors in the thalamocortical system. Inhibits reuptake of catecholamines (serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine). Interacts with mu and kappa opioid receptors.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset: IV 30-60 sec, IM 3-4 min; Duration 10-20 min; Active metabolite: norketamine (1/3 to 1/5 potency); Hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4 and CYP2B6; Elimination half-life 2-3 hours.", "pearls": "'Dissociative anesthesia': Patient appears awake with open eyes, slow nystagmic gaze, intact corneal and pharyngeal reflexes, but is profoundly amnestic and analgesic. Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac output (indirect sympathomimetic via catecholamine reuptake block; directly a weak myocardial depressant if catecholamines are exhausted). Potent bronchodilator via beta-2 agonism. Preserves spontaneous respiratory drive. Emergence delirium/hallucinations in ~15-30% of adults (pre-treat with IV Midazolam). Salivation is prominent (combine with Glycopyrronium or Atropine).", "contraindications": "Uncontrolled severe hypertension, pheochromocytoma, pre-existing elevated intracranial pressure with compromised CSF dynamics, penetrating eye injuries, acute psychosis.", "dosageForms": "Solution for injection: 10 mg/mL, 50 mg/mL, and 100 mg/mL vials (IV, IM, oral, intranasal).", "monitoring": "Continuous blood pressure, heart rate, ECG, pulse oximetry, airway secretions."}

name: Midazolam
description: {"atc": "N01CD08", "indications": "Preoperative anxiolysis and anterograde amnesia; procedural sedation; induction of anesthesia (high dose); continuous sedation in intensive care; status epilepticus rescue. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors, increasing channel opening frequency in the limbic system, cortex, and thalamus.", "pharmacokinetics": "Water-soluble at acidic pH (ampoule pH 3.5), lipid-soluble at physiological pH (pH 7.4), allowing rapid crossing of the blood-brain barrier. Onset IV 1-2 min; Elimination half-life 1.5-2.5 hours; Hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4 to 1-hydroxymidazolam (active metabolite; accumulates in renal failure).", "pearls": "Exceptional anterograde amnesia with preserved retrograde memory: patients typically have no recollection of unpleasant perioperative events. Synergistic respiratory depression when combined with opioids. Reversible with the competitive antagonist Flumazenil (0.2 mg IV titrated, beware resedation due to shorter half-life of flumazenil ~1 hour). Paradoxical agitation occurs in <1% (especially children and elderly).", "contraindications": "Severe acute respiratory insufficiency; myasthenia gravis; sleep apnea syndrome; acute narrow-angle glaucoma; severe hepatic impairment.", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 1 mg/mL, 2 mg/mL, and 5 mg/mL ampoules; oral syrup 2 mg/mL (pediatric pre-medication); buccal liquid.", "monitoring": "Continuous SpO2, respiratory rate, sedation score (RASS), blood pressure, ECG."}

name: Lidocaine
description: {"atc": "N01BB02", "indications": "Local and regional infiltration anesthesia; peripheral nerve blocks; spinal and epidural anesthesia; topical mucosal anesthesia; systemic IV lidocaine infusion for perioperative analgesia; Class Ib antiarrhythmic for ventricular arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia/VF). WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Voltage-gated sodium channel blocker (Nav1.5, Nav1.7): reversibly binds the intracellular S6 segment of domain IV, blocking sodium influx and halting axonal action potential generation and propagation. Preferentially binds active/open and inactivated states (use-dependent block).", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid onset (2-5 min); Intermediate duration (60-120 min plain, extended to 240 min with epinephrine 1:200,000); Hepatic de-ethylation by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 to monoethylglycinexylidide (MEGX); Elimination half-life 1.5-2 hours; Maximum dose: 3-4.5 mg/kg plain, up to 7 mg/kg with epinephrine.", "pearls": "⚠️ Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST): Initial signs include circumoral numbness, metallic taste in mouth, tinnitus, dizziness, visual disturbances, progressing to muscle twitching, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and cardiovascular collapse (ventricular arrhythmias, asystole). Emergency antidote: 20% Lipid Emulsion (Intralipid: 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 1 min, followed by 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion). Addition of Epinephrine (adrenaline 1:200,000) causes local vasoconstriction, reducing systemic absorption, prolonging block duration, and providing a marker for accidental intravascular injection.", "contraindications": "Complete heart block, severe sinoatrial block; known allergy to amino-amides; application of epinephrine-containing solutions to end-artery anatomical areas (digits, penis, nose, ears - risk of ischemic necrosis).", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 0.5%, 1%, 2% (with and without Epinephrine 1:200,000); 4% topical solution; 5% ointment; 10% oral spray; 2.5% Lidocaine + 2.5% Prilocaine (EMLA cream).", "monitoring": "Continuous ECG during blocks, mental status check during injection, signs of LAST, blood pressure, local site assessment."}

name: Bupivacaine
description: {"atc": "N01BB01", "indications": "Spinal (subarachnoid) anesthesia for cesarean section, lower limb and pelvic surgery; epidural analgesia (labor, postoperative pain); major plexus and peripheral nerve blocks; wound infiltration. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Amino-amide local anesthetic. High-affinity blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels. Dissociates very slowly from cardiac sodium channels during diastole ('fast-in, slow-out' kinetics), conferring profound cardiotoxicity.", "pharmacokinetics": "Slow onset (10-20 min); Long duration (3-8 hours depending on route); 95% protein bound (to alpha-1-acid glycoprotein); Hepatic metabolism by CYP3A4; Elimination half-life 2.7-3.5 hours; Maximum single dose: 2 mg/kg (up to 150 mg plain, 175-200 mg with adrenaline).", "pearls": "Marked cardiotoxicity compared to lidocaine (CC/CNS ratio is low ~2.0 vs 7.0 for lidocaine): toxic doses trigger refractory ventricular arrhythmias and electromechanical dissociation before neurological warning signs appear. Binds tightly to cardiac sodium channels and interferes with mitochondrial ATP synthesis. Accidental IV injection during labor epidural is a major historical cause of maternal cardiac arrest. Treatment: Resuscitation + Immediate 20% Lipid Emulsion rescue. Hyperbaric Bupivacaine (0.5% in 8% dextrose) used for predictable gravity-guided spinal anesthesia.", "contraindications": "Intravenous regional anesthesia (Bier's block - ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED due to risk of fatal tourniquet leak); severe cardiac conduction block; localized skin infection at puncture site; hypovolemia in neuraxial anesthesia.", "dosageForms": "Injectable: 0.25% (2.5 mg/mL) and 0.5% (5 mg/mL) isobaric; 0.5% hyperbaric (heavy with 80 mg/mL glucose); with/without Epinephrine 1:200,000.", "monitoring": "Aspiration before every 3-5 mL increment; ECG monitoring; frequent blood pressure (hypotension watch in spinal anesthesia); dermatomal sensory level testing (cold/touch)."}

name: Ropivacaine
description: {"atc": "N01BB09", "indications": "Epidural anesthesia and labor analgesia; major peripheral nerve blocks; continuous wound catheter infusions; postoperative pain management.", "mechanism": "Pure S-(-)-enantiomer amino-amide local anesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in sensory and motor nerve fibers.", "pharmacokinetics": "Intermediate-to-slow onset (10-15 min); Long duration (3-6 hours); 94% protein binding; Hepatic metabolism by CYP1A2; Elimination half-life 1.8-2.0 hours; Maximum single dose: 3 mg/kg (up to 225-300 mg).", "pearls": "Engineered as a single enantiomer to reduce cardiotoxicity and neurotoxicity compared to racemic bupivacaine. Displays clinical sensory-motor differentiation: provides reliable sensory analgesia with significantly less motor block at low concentrations (0.1-0.2%), making it ideal for walking epidurals and continuous nerve block infusions. Higher threshold for LAST than bupivacaine.", "contraindications": "Intravenous regional anesthesia (Bier's block); known amino-amide hypersensitivity; severe hepatic failure.", "dosageForms": "Injectable: 2 mg/mL (0.2%), 5 mg/mL (0.5%), 7.5 mg/mL (0.75%), and 10 mg/mL (1%) in 10 mL and 20 mL ampoules/polyamps.", "monitoring": "Frequent hemodynamic monitoring, motor power assessment (Bromage scale), continuous sensory level tracking."}

name: Suxamethonium
description: {"atc": "M03AB01", "indications": "Depolarizing neuromuscular blockade for Rapid Sequence Induction (RSI) intubation; emergency airway control; electroconvulsive therapy (ECT); brief surgical procedures requiring profound muscle relaxation. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Synthetic dicholine ester that binds nicotinic acetylcholine (nACh) receptors at the neuromuscular motor endplate, causing prolonged depolarization. Produces Phase I block (muscle fasciculations followed by flaccid paralysis) and, with large/repeated doses, Phase II block (desensitization mimicking non-depolarizing block).", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid onset: 30-60 seconds (fastest of all muscle relaxants); Brief duration: 5-10 minutes; Rapidly hydrolyzed in plasma by pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase / BChE).", "pearls": "Triggers muscle fasciculations prior to paralysis, causing postoperative myalgia (blunted by small pre-curarization dose of rocuronium). Transiently increases serum potassium by 0.5 mEq/L (catastrophic hyperkalemia up to 8-10 mEq/L leading to cardiac arrest in denervation states: burn victims >24 hrs, spinal cord transection, prolonged ICU immobilization, muscular dystrophies). ⚠️ Potent trigger of Malignant Hyperthermia when combined with volatile anesthetics. Increases intraocular, intragastric, and intracranial pressure. Prolonged apnea occurs in atypical pseudocholinesterase (Dibucaine number testing).", "contraindications": "Major burns (>24 hrs post-injury), extensive crush injury, spinal cord injury/paraplegia, muscular dystrophy (Duchenne's), hyperkalemia, personal/family history of malignant hyperthermia, open globe eye injury.", "dosageForms": "Solution for injection: 50 mg/mL (100 mg in 2 mL ampoules), requires cold chain storage (2-8°C).", "monitoring": "Cardiac monitor (bradycardia on repeat doses, treat with atropine), serum potassium in high-risk patients, continuous peripheral nerve stimulator (TOF), core temperature."}

name: Rocuronium
description: {"atc": "M03AC09", "indications": "Intermediate-acting aminosteroid neuromuscular blocking agent for routine endotracheal intubation and surgical muscle relaxation; alternative to suxamethonium for Rapid Sequence Induction (RSI) at high dose (1.2 mg/kg). WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Competitive antagonist at postjunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors of the skeletal neuromuscular junction, preventing acetylcholine binding and depolarization.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset: 60-90 seconds (standard intubating dose 0.6 mg/kg), 45-60 seconds (RSI dose 1.2 mg/kg); Clinical duration: 30-45 minutes; Elimination primarily biliary (~70%) and renal (~30%); Minimal hepatic metabolism.", "pearls": "RSI workhorse when suxamethonium is contraindicated (burns, hyperkalemia, denervation). Unlike suxamethonium, does not trigger malignant hyperthermia, hyperkalemia, or muscle fasciculations. Complete, rapid, and predictable chemical encapsulation and reversal within 2-3 minutes using Sugammadex (2-16 mg/kg depending on block depth). Prolonged duration in hepatic failure, renal failure, and hypothermia.", "contraindications": "Known hypersensitivity to rocuronium or bromide ion.", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 10 mg/mL (50 mg in 5 mL vials). Stable at room temperature (<25°C) for up to 12 weeks, otherwise refrigerated (2-8°C).", "monitoring": "Quantitative Train-of-Four (TOF) ratio monitoring on adductor pollicis muscle; core temperature; recovery confirmed before extubation (TOF ratio >= 0.9)."}

name: Vecuronium
description: {"atc": "M03AC03", "indications": "Intermediate-acting aminosteroid muscle relaxant for surgical endotracheal intubation and skeletal muscle relaxation in general anesthesia. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Competitive antagonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors of the motor endplate.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset: 2.5-3 minutes; Clinical duration: 25-35 minutes; Hepatic metabolism (active 3-hydroxy metabolite, 50% potency, accumulates in renal failure); Biliary excretion 40-50%, renal 30%.", "pearls": "Exceptional cardiovascular stability: zero histamine release, zero vagolytic activity, zero change in heart rate or blood pressure. Reversible with Neostigmine (+ Glycopyrrolate) or Sugammadex. Preferred in patients with coronary artery disease and valvular heart disease where tachycardia must be strictly avoided.", "contraindications": "Severe hypersensitivity to vecuronium.", "dosageForms": "Lyophilized powder for injection: 4 mg and 10 mg vials (reconstituted with water for injection; stable at room temperature).", "monitoring": "TOF monitoring, train-of-four ratio >= 0.9 before reversal/extubation."}

name: Atracurium
description: {"atc": "M03AC04", "indications": "Intermediate-acting benzylisoquinolinium muscle relaxant for endotracheal intubation and muscle relaxation in surgical patients, especially those with renal and/or hepatic failure. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Competitive antagonism of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset: 2-2.5 minutes; Duration: 30-40 minutes; Spontaneous organ-independent breakdown via Hofmann elimination (temperature and pH dependent chemical cleavage) and non-specific plasma esterase hydrolysis (~60-70%).", "pearls": "Drug of choice in end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and severe liver failure due to organ-independent Hofmann elimination. Rapid IV bolus administration causes dose-dependent mast cell degranulation and histamine release, resulting in skin flushing, bronchospasm, and hypotension (administer slowly over 30-60 seconds). Breakdown product 'Laudanosine' crosses blood-brain barrier with theoretical pro-convulsant potential in prolonged ICU infusions.", "contraindications": "Known severe allergic sensitivity to atracurium or benzenesulfonic acid.", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 10 mg/mL (25 mg in 2.5 mL, 50 mg in 5 mL ampoules); cold chain storage required (2-8°C).", "monitoring": "TOF monitor, blood pressure monitoring during injection, core temperature and arterial pH (hypothermia and acidosis prolong Hofmann elimination)."}

name: Cisatracurium

name: Neostigmine
description: {"atc": "N07AA01", "indications": "Reversal of non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockade at the conclusion of surgery; treatment of myasthenia gravis; acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome). WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Quaternary carbamate acetylcholinesterase inhibitor: reversibly carbamylates the active esteratic site of acetylcholinesterase, preventing breakdown of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and increasing ACh competition at the motor endplate.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset: 1-3 minutes; Peak effect: 7-10 minutes; Duration: 40-60 minutes; Elimination half-life 50-90 minutes; 50% renal excretion unchanged, 50% hepatic metabolism.", "pearls": "MUST always be co-administered with an antimuscarinic anticholinergic (Glycopyrrolate 0.2 mg per 1.0 mg neostigmine or Atropine 0.4-0.6 mg per 1.0 mg neostigmine) to block systemic parasympathetic muscarinic overstimulation (bradycardia, asystole, bronchospasm, salivation, miosis, increased peristalsis). Ceiling effect: administering neostigmine when TOF count is 0 ('deep block') causes paradoxical neuromuscular weakness and fails to reverse block. Only administer when at least 2, preferably 4 twitches are visible on TOF.", "contraindications": "Mechanical gastrointestinal or urinary tract obstruction; peritonitis; known hypersensitivity to neostigmine; prior administration of suxamethonium with depolarizing block (prolongs Phase I block!).", "dosageForms": "Injectable: 0.5 mg/mL and 2.5 mg/mL in 1 mL and 5 mL ampoules; pre-mixed Neostigmine 2.5 mg + Glycopyrrolate 0.5 mg in 1 mL ampoules.", "monitoring": "Continuous ECG (severe bradycardia watch), train-of-four ratio (target >0.9 before extubation), airway secretions, auscultation for wheezing."}

name: Sugammadex
description: {"atc": "V03AB35", "indications": "Routine and emergency reversal of neuromuscular blockade induced by aminosteroid muscle relaxants (Rocuronium > Vecuronium) in adult and pediatric surgery.", "mechanism": "Modified gamma-cyclodextrin: uniquely designed lipophilic core encapsulates and chemically chelates the lipophilic steroid rings of rocuronium and vecuronium in a 1:1 tight molecular complex. Decreases free plasma concentration to zero, driving rapid dissociation of rocuronium from postjunctional receptors.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset: Complete reversal within 1.5 to 3 minutes; Elimination half-life ~2 hours; Excreted >95% unchanged by the kidneys.", "pearls": "Revolutionized anesthesia safety: enables immediate reversal of deep block or immediate rescue in a 'Cannot Intubate, Cannot Oxygenate' (CICO) crisis after 1.2 mg/kg rocuronium (emergency dose: 16 mg/kg IV). Works independently of acetylcholinesterase and does not cause muscarinic side effects (zero bradycardia, zero bronchospasm, no anticholinergic needed). ⚠️ Drug Interaction: Binds and neutralizes steroidal oral contraceptives (patients taking oral contraception must use an alternative non-hormonal barrier method for 7 days post-dose). Rare hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis (~0.3%).", "contraindications": "Severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30 mL/min / hemodialysis - complex is dialyzable but prolonged retention occurs); severe hypersensitivity to sugammadex.", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 100 mg/mL in 2 mL (200 mg) and 5 mL (500 mg) vials.", "monitoring": "Objective TOF monitoring, advice regarding hormonal contraceptive backup, observation for rare hypersensitivity reactions."}

name: Atropine
description: {"atc": "A03BA01", "indications": "Emergency treatment of severe symptomatic bradycardia and AV nodal heart block (ACLS algorithm); antidote for organophosphate, carbamate, and nerve agent poisoning; antisialagogue (reduction of airway secretions); co-administered with anticholinesterases. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Competitive, reversible antagonist of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (M1, M2, M3, M4, M5). Blocks vagal cardiac parasympathetic tone at M2 receptors in the SA and AV nodes, increasing sinus rate and AV conduction velocity.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset IV 1-2 minutes; Duration of vagolytic effect 1-2 hours; Hepatic metabolism ~50%; Renal excretion ~30-50% unchanged; Crosses blood-brain barrier and placenta.", "pearls": "⚠️ Paradoxical bradycardia occurs with low doses (<0.5 mg IV) due to central vagal stimulation or blockade of presynaptic inhibitory M1 receptors on postganglionic parasympathetic nerves (always give >=0.5 mg in adults). High doses cause classic 'anticholinergic toxidrome': 'Blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, red as a beet, hot as a hare, dry as a bone' (mydriasis, delirium, cutaneous flushing, hyperthermia, dry mouth/skin, urinary retention). In organophosphate poisoning, titrate until pulmonary secretions are clear and bronchospasm resolves.", "contraindications": "Acute narrow-angle glaucoma; obstructive uropathy (prostatic hypertrophy); mechanical gastrointestinal obstruction, paralytic ileus, severe ulcerative colitis/toxic megacolon; myasthenia gravis (unless used to treat cholinergic crisis).", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 0.5 mg/mL, 0.6 mg/mL, and 1 mg/mL ampoules.", "monitoring": "Continuous ECG/heart rate, pupillary diameter, body temperature, airway secretion dryness, bladder palpation."}

name: Glycopyrronium
description: {"atc": "A03AB02", "indications": "Preoperative and perioperative antisialagogue; prevention of muscarinic side effects during reversal of neuromuscular block with neostigmine; chronic drooling; COPD maintenance.", "mechanism": "Synthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic agent. Competitively blocks peripheral muscarinic receptors (M1-M3).", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset IV 1-2 minutes; Duration of vagal block 2-3 hours, antisialagogue effect up to 7 hours; Poor lipid solubility due to quaternary structure; Does NOT cross blood-brain barrier or placenta.", "pearls": "Ideal perioperative antimuscarinic: lacks the central nervous system side effects of atropine (no central anticholinergic syndrome, sedation, confusion, or delirium), making it preferred in elderly surgical patients. Less prone to causing tachycardia than atropine at equipotent antisialagogue doses. Does not cross the placenta, protecting the fetus during maternal administration.", "contraindications": "Glaucoma (narrow-angle); obstructive gastrointestinal disease; severe paralytic ileus; obstructive uropathy; tachycardia secondary to cardiac failure.", "dosageForms": "Injectable: 0.2 mg/mL in 1 mL and 3 mL ampoules.", "monitoring": "Heart rate, ECG, dryness of oral secretions."}

name: Paracetamol
description: {"atc": "N02BE01", "indications": "Mild to moderate nociceptive pain; antipyretic for fever; multimodal perioperative analgesia backbone (opioid-sparing); first-line analgesic in osteoarthritis and pediatric febrile illness. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Central inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis through potent inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase variants (peroxidase active site of COX-1/COX-2 in environments with low peroxide concentrations, e.g. brain/spinal cord). Activates descending serotonergic inhibitory pain pathways; metabolite AM404 inhibits endocannabinoid reuptake.", "pharmacokinetics": "Bioavailability: Oral ~80%, IV 100%, Rectal variable (30-65%); Onset: Oral 30 min, IV 5-15 min; Peak analgesia ~1 hr; Half-life 2-3 hrs; Hepatic metabolism: 90% via glucuronidation and sulfation, 5-10% oxidized by CYP2E1 to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI).", "pearls": "Lacks clinically significant peripheral anti-inflammatory activity, gastric mucosal injury, or platelet inhibition (safe in peptic ulcer disease and bleeding diathesis). ⚠️ Hepatotoxicity in overdose (>150 mg/kg or >10-12 g in adults): Glutathione stores are depleted, leaving toxic reactive NAPQI to bind hepatic macromolecules, causing centrilobular hepatic necrosis. Antidote: Intravenous N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) restores intracellular hepatic glutathione (most effective if started within 8 hours). Maximum daily adult dose: 4,000 mg (reduce to 2,000-3,000 mg in chronic alcohol abuse, malnutrition, liver cirrhosis).", "contraindications": "Severe acute active hepatocellular insufficiency or decompensated liver failure; known severe hypersensitivity.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 500 mg, 650 mg; oral suspension: 120 mg/5 mL, 250 mg/5 mL; IV infusion: 10 mg/mL (1,000 mg in 100 mL vials); rectal suppositories: 125 mg, 250 mg, 500 mg.", "monitoring": "Cumulative 24-hour dose tracking; LFTs, INR, and paracetamol serum level (Rumack-Matthew nomogram) in suspected overdose."}

name: Acetylsalicylic acid
description: {"atc": "N02BA01", "indications": "Low-dose (75-150 mg): Secondary prevention of cardiovascular events (acute coronary syndromes, post-PCI, ischemic stroke, TIA); High-dose (300-1,000 mg): Mild-to-moderate inflammatory pain, acute migraine, rheumatic fever, Kawasaki disease. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Irreversible acetylation of serine 529 in COX-1 and serine 516 in COX-2. Irreversibly inhibits platelet thromboxane A2 (TXA2) synthesis for the entire lifespan of the platelet (7-10 days), blocking platelet aggregation.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapidly absorbed in stomach and upper small intestine; Hydrolyzed by plasma and tissue esterases to salicylic acid (half-life 15-20 min); Salicylate half-life is dose-dependent (2-3 hrs at low dose, up to 15-30 hrs at toxic anti-inflammatory doses due to hepatic clearance saturation); Renal excretion.", "pearls": "⚠️ Reye's Syndrome: Strictly contraindicated in children and adolescents under 16 years with viral illnesses (varicella, influenza) due to risk of microvesicular fatty liver disease and encephalopathy (exception: Kawasaki disease). ⚠️ Samter's Triad (Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease / AERD): Asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, and bronchospasm upon COX-1 inhibition (shunt to 5-lipoxygenase pathway and leukotriene synthesis). ⚠️ Salicylate Poisoning: Tinnitus, respiratory alkalosis (direct medullary center stimulation) followed by high anion gap metabolic acidosis (uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation); treat with urine alkalinization (IV NaHCO3) and hemodialysis.", "contraindications": "Children <16 years with viral infection; active peptic ulceration; hemophilia/bleeding disorders; severe renal/hepatic failure; 3rd trimester pregnancy; history of AERD.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 75 mg, 81 mg, 100 mg (enteric-coated cardio-aspirin); 300 mg, 500 mg soluble/effervescent tablets.", "monitoring": "Stool occult blood, bleeding time/platelet count, renal function, serum salicylate level in toxicity."}

name: Ibuprofen
description: {"atc": "M01AE01", "indications": "Mild to moderate pain, dysmenorrhea, dental pain, headache; musculoskeletal inflammation (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis); closure of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in preterm neonates; fever reduction. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Reversible, competitive non-selective inhibitor of both cyclo-oxygenase-1 (COX-1) and cyclo-oxygenase-2 (COX-2), decreasing peripheral and central prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) synthesis.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid absorption (peak plasma concentration 1-2 hours); 99% plasma protein bound; Hepatic CYP2C9 and CYP2C8 metabolism; Elimination half-life 1.8-2.0 hours; Renal excretion of metabolites.", "pearls": "Generally regarded as the non-selective NSAID with the lowest gastrointestinal toxicity profile at standard over-the-counter doses (<=1,200 mg/day). Reversibly inhibits platelet aggregation (antiplatelet effect ends when drug is cleared, unlike aspirin). Can competitively interfere with the cardioprotective antiplatelet effect of aspirin (take aspirin 30 min before ibuprofen). ⚠️ Renal Papillary Necrosis & Triple Whammy: Combination of NSAID (afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction via prostaglandin block) + ACE inhibitor/ARB (efferent arteriolar vasodilation) + Diuretic causes acute prerenal kidney failure.", "contraindications": "Active gastrointestinal bleeding or peptic ulcer disease; severe congestive heart failure (NYHA III-IV); severe renal impairment; third trimester of pregnancy (premature closure of fetal ductus arteriosus).", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets/capsules: 200 mg, 400 mg, 600 mg, 800 mg; oral suspension: 100 mg/5 mL; topical gel 5%; IV infusion (for PDA closure / acute pain).", "monitoring": "Blood pressure (can elevate BP by 3-5 mmHg), serum creatinine and eGFR, GI symptom review, complete blood count."}

name: Naproxen
description: {"atc": "M01AE02", "indications": "Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gouty arthritis, tendonitis, dysmenorrhea, acute migraine attacks.", "mechanism": "Reversible non-selective inhibition of COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes, suppressing synthesis of pro-inflammatory prostaglandins and thromboxanes.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid oral absorption; Long elimination half-life of 12-17 hours (enables twice-daily dosing); Highly protein bound (99%); Hepatic metabolism via CYP2C9 and CYP1A2.", "pearls": "Demonstrates the lowest cardiovascular risk profile (myocardial infarction and stroke) among non-selective NSAIDs, likely due to sustained platelet COX-1 suppression throughout its 24-hour dosing interval. However, carries a moderately high gastrointestinal ulceration risk (co-prescribe with a PPI like Omeprazole in patients >65 years or with ulcer history).", "contraindications": "Active peptic ulcer disease; history of recurrent GI bleeding; severe heart failure; severe renal impairment; 3rd trimester pregnancy.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 250 mg, 375 mg, 500 mg; Naproxen sodium 275 mg, 550 mg (faster absorption); oral suspension 125 mg/5 mL.", "monitoring": "Renal panel, blood pressure, CBC, symptoms of dyspepsia or melena."}

name: Diclofenac
description: {"atc": "M01AB05", "indications": "Acute postoperative pain; renal colic (first-line in emergency settings); acute migraine; flare-ups of osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis; topical therapy for localized joint pain. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Preferential inhibition of COX-2 over COX-1; suppresses prostaglandin synthesis and reduces leukocyte intracellular arachidonic acid concentrations.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid absorption; Undergoes ~50% first-pass hepatic metabolism; Short elimination half-life 1-2 hours, but accumulates in synovial fluid where concentrations remain high for >11 hours; Hepatic CYP2C9 metabolism.", "pearls": "Exceptional efficacy in renal colic (relieves ureteric smooth muscle spasm and decreases renal capsular pressure by reducing afferent renal blood flow). ⚠️ Highest cardiovascular thrombotic risk among standard non-selective NSAIDs (similar risk profile to selective COX-2 inhibitors; avoid in patients with ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, and cerebrovascular disease). High incidence of transient elevation in hepatic transaminases (ALT/AST). Topical gel formulations achieve high synovial levels with <10% systemic absorption.", "contraindications": "Ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, history of stroke/TIA, congestive heart failure (NYHA II-IV); active GI ulcer/bleeding; severe hepatic/renal impairment.", "dosageForms": "Enteric-coated tablets: 25 mg, 50 mg; sustained release: 75 mg, 100 mg; ampoules for IM/IV injection: 75 mg in 3 mL; topical gel 1% and 2.32%; eye drops 0.1%.", "monitoring": "Baseline and periodic liver function tests (LFTs), blood pressure, serum creatinine, cardiovascular risk assessment."}

name: Ketorolac
description: {"atc": "M01AB15", "indications": "Short-term management (MAXIMUM 5 consecutive days) of moderate-to-severe acute postoperative and trauma pain; acute renal colic; ophthalmic drops for seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and post-cataract inflammation.", "mechanism": "Potent non-selective COX-1 and COX-2 inhibitor with marked analgesic potency comparable to low-to-moderate dose opioids, without sedative or respiratory depressant effects.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid onset IV/IM 10-30 min; Peak effect 1-2 hours; Duration 4-6 hours; Elimination half-life 4-6 hours; 99% protein bound; Excreted primarily unchanged by kidneys.", "pearls": "⚠️ Severe Black Box Warning: STRICT 5-DAY MAXIMUM TREATMENT DURATION across all routes combined. High incidence of life-threatening gastrointestinal perforation, peptic ulceration, operative site bleeding (due to potent COX-1 inhibition of platelet TXA2), and acute renal failure. Never give preoperatively when hemostasis is critical. Dose must be reduced by 50% in patients >=65 years, weighing <50 kg, or with mildly elevated serum creatinine.", "contraindications": "Active or history of GI bleeding/perforation; advanced renal impairment or at risk for renal failure; suspected cerebrovascular bleeding; epidural or intrathecal administration; labor and delivery; combination with other NSAIDs.", "dosageForms": "Injectable: 10 mg/mL, 15 mg/mL, 30 mg/mL in 1 mL ampoules; oral tablets 10 mg (only for continuation of parenteral therapy); ophthalmic solution 0.5%.", "monitoring": "Strict count of treatment days (never exceed 5), urine output, serum BUN/creatinine, surgical drain volume, hemoglobin/hematocrit."}

name: Morphine
description: {"atc": "N02AA01", "indications": "Gold-standard opioid for severe acute pain (trauma, surgical, burns); chronic cancer pain (WHO Pain Ladder Step 3); acute pulmonary edema (reduces preload and anxiety); acute myocardial infarction pain. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Strong full agonist at mu-opioid receptors (MOR) coupled to Gi/o proteins: closes voltage-gated calcium channels presynaptically (reducing neurotransmitter release: substance P, glutamate) and opens G-protein coupled inward-rectifying potassium channels (GIRK) postsynaptically, hyperpolarizing pain transmission neurons in the dorsal horn.", "pharmacokinetics": "Oral bioavailability ~20-40% (high first-pass metabolism); Elimination half-life 2-3 hours; Hepatic glucuronidation to Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G, 60%, neurotoxic/hyperalgesic) and Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G, 10%, 2-4x more potent analgesic than morphine). Both metabolites accumulate significantly in renal failure.", "pearls": "⚠️ Renal Failure Danger: Accumulation of active M6G in renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min) causes severe delayed narcosis and fatal respiratory depression; switch to Fentanyl or Buprenorphine. Causes mast cell degranulation via non-immune mechanisms, triggering histamine-induced hypotension, flushing, and pruritus. Pinpoint pupils (miosis) and constipation show NO tolerance over time (always prescribe a stimulant laxative like Senna). Respiratory depression is mediated via reduced medullary response to hypercapnia.", "contraindications": "Severe respiratory depression, acute asthma attack, paralytic ileus, raised intracranial pressure with hypoventilation, severe renal failure (M6G toxicity), acute biliary colic (causes sphincter of Oddi spasm).", "dosageForms": "Immediate release tablets: 10 mg, 20 mg; sustained release: 10 mg, 30 mg, 60 mg, 100 mg; oral solution: 10 mg/5 mL, 20 mg/mL; IV/SC ampoules: 10 mg/mL, 15 mg/mL; preservative-free ampoules for epidural/intrathecal use.", "monitoring": "Respiratory rate (<10 breaths/min indicates toxicity), sedation scale (POSS), pupillary constriction, bowel movements (constipation protocol), pain score."}

name: Codeine
description: {"atc": "N02AA59", "indications": "Mild to moderate pain (Step 2 on WHO Pain Ladder, often combined with Paracetamol); cough suppression (antitussive). WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Weak opioid prodrug. Has low intrinsic affinity for mu-opioid receptors; ~10% is converted into active morphine by hepatic cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6).", "pharmacokinetics": "Good oral bioavailability (~50%); Half-life 2.5-3 hours; Renal excretion of glucuronides and free morphine.", "pearls": "⚠️ CYP2D6 Pharmacogenomic Danger: 'Ultra-rapid metabolizers' (duplication of CYP2D6 gene, up to 10-29% in North African and Middle Eastern populations) rapidly convert codeine to lethal toxic levels of morphine (cases of fatal pediatric respiratory arrest post-tonsillectomy and maternal-infant toxicity via breast milk). 'Poor metabolizers' (~7-10% of Caucasians) lack CYP2D6 activity and experience zero analgesic benefit. Black box warning: strictly contraindicated in children <12 years and post-tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy in patients <18 years.", "contraindications": "Children <12 years; post-tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy in children <18 years; nursing mothers; known ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolizers; severe respiratory insufficiency.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 15 mg, 30 mg, 60 mg; Codeine + Paracetamol combination (30/500 mg Co-codamol); cough syrup 15 mg/5 mL.", "monitoring": "Respiratory rate, signs of opioid toxicity, bowel movements."}

name: Fentanyl
description: {"atc": "N01AH01", "indications": "Intraoperative analgesia during balanced general anesthesia; Patient-Controlled Analgesia (PCA); breakthrough cancer pain; transdermal patches for chronic severe stable cancer pain. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Potent synthetic phenylpiperidine full agonist at mu-opioid receptors. Approximately 50 to 100 times more potent than morphine.", "pharmacokinetics": "Extremely lipophilic; IV onset 1-2 minutes; Duration of single IV bolus is short (30-60 min) due to rapid redistribution into skeletal muscle and fat; Hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4 to inactive norfentanyl; Zero active metabolites (safe in renal failure!); Transdermal patch has 12-24 hr depot delay and 72-hr duration.", "pearls": "Analgesic of choice in renal impairment because it lacks active toxic metabolites. name: Naloxone
description: {"atc": "V03AB15", "indications": "Emergency reversal of life-threatening opioid overdose (respiratory depression, coma); reversal of unwanted opioid-induced perioperative side effects; diagnostic challenge in suspected opioid coma. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Pure competitive antagonist at mu, kappa, and delta opioid receptors, with highest affinity at mu receptors. Rapidly displaces opioid agonists from receptor binding sites.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset: IV 1-2 minutes, IM/SC 2-5 minutes, Intranasal 2-3 minutes; Duration of action: 30-90 minutes (dangerously short compared to long-acting opioids!); Hepatic glucuronidation to naloxone-3-glucuronide; Elimination half-life ~60-90 minutes.", "pearls": "⚠️ Renarcotization / Relapse Danger: The elimination half-life of Naloxone (60-90 min) is significantly shorter than that of most opioids (Morphine 3-4 hrs, Methadone 24-36 hrs, SR formulations). Patients can wake up, appear fully alert, and then lapse back into fatal respiratory depression 1-2 hours later. Continuous observation for >=4-6 hours is mandatory; repeated doses or a continuous infusion may be required. Rapid high-dose reversal in opioid-dependent individuals triggers severe acute withdrawal: sympathetic storm, severe hypertension, ventricular arrhythmias, flash pulmonary edema, and extreme agitation. Titrate in small IV increments (40-80 mcg every 2 min) until respiratory rate reaches 10-12 breaths/min.", "contraindications": "Known hypersensitivity to naloxone.", "dosageForms": "Injectable: 0.4 mg/mL and 1 mg/mL ampoules; pre-filled emergency auto-injectors; intranasal spray (Narcan): 4 mg per actuation.", "monitoring": "Respiratory rate, SpO2, level of consciousness, duration of opioid clearance, signs of precipitated withdrawal."}

name: Amoxicillin
description: {"atc": "J01CA04", "indications": "First-line aminopenicillin for acute otitis media, community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial sinusitis, streptococcal pharyngitis, uncomplicated urinary tract infections, and Helicobacter pylori eradication. name: Ceftriaxone
description: {"atc": "J01DD04", "indications": "Third-generation cephalosporin for bacterial meningitis, community-acquired and hospital pneumonia, pyelonephritis, severe typhoid fever, disseminated gonococcal infection, and surgical prophylaxis. Displaces bilirubin from albumin, causing kernicterus in neonates. name: Gentamicin
description: {"atc": "J01GB03", "indications": "Severe Gram-negative aerobic bacillary infections (Pseudomonas, Enterobacteriaceae); synergistic combination with ampicillin for enterococcal/streptococcal infective endocarditis; neonatal sepsis. WHO EML Access Group.", "mechanism": "Aminoglycoside: irreversibly binds the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA genetic code and premature termination of protein synthesis. Highly bactericidal with concentration-dependent killing and prolonged post-antibiotic effect (PAE).", "pharmacokinetics": "Polar polycationic molecule: essentially zero oral absorption (requires IV/IM); Poor intracellular and CSF penetration; Excreted 100% unchanged via glomerular filtration; Half-life 2-3 hours (dramatically prolonged in renal failure).", "pearls": "Concentration-dependent killing: once-daily extended-interval dosing (5-7 mg/kg/day) maximizes peak-to-MIC ratio (>8-10) while allowing trough concentrations to drop <1 mcg/mL, minimizing toxicity. ⚠️ Ototoxicity (vestibular > cochlear damage): Irreversible destruction of sensory hair cells via free radical generation (accumulates in endolymph). ⚠️ Nephrotoxicity: Reversible non-oliguric acute kidney injury due to uptake into proximal tubular cells (megalin/cubilin receptor-mediated). Curare-like neuromuscular blockade: inhibits presynaptic acetylcholine release (contraindicated in Myasthenia Gravis).", "contraindications": "Myasthenia gravis; pre-existing severe vestibulocochlear damage; concurrent use of other potent ototoxic/nephrotoxic drugs (furosemide, cisplatin).", "dosageForms": "Solution for injection: 40 mg/mL (80 mg in 2 mL ampoules); ophthalmic drops 0.3%.", "monitoring": "Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM): trough level <1 mcg/mL (immediately prior to next dose) to prevent toxicity; peak level 15-20 mcg/mL; serum creatinine twice weekly; vestibular/hearing assessment."}

name: Ciprofloxacin
description: {"atc": "J01MA02", "indications": "Complicated urinary tract infections, pyelonephritis, bacterial prostatitis, traveler's diarrhea (shigellosis, salmonellosis), intra-abdominal infections, pulmonary Pseudomonas in cystic fibrosis, anthrax prophylaxis. WHO EML Watch Group.", "mechanism": "Fluoroquinolone: bactericidal inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, preventing DNA supercoiling, transcription, and replication.", "pharmacokinetics": "Excellent oral bioavailability (70-80%); Large volume of distribution; Moderate hepatic metabolism; Elimination predominantly renal; Half-life 4 hours.", "pearls": "Oral route provides tissue levels comparable to IV administration. Chelation interaction: Polyvalent cations (calcium, iron, aluminum, magnesium antacids) reduce oral absorption by >90% (space by >=2 hours). ⚠️ Tendinitis & Tendon Rupture (especially Achilles tendon): Risk highest in elderly patients and those taking systemic corticosteroids. ⚠️ Prolongation of QT Interval: Increases risk of Torsades de Pointes. ⚠️ Neuropsychiatric Effects & Aortic Dissection warnings: Can trigger seizures, confusion, hallucinations, and peripheral neuropathy.", "contraindications": "Concurrent use of tizanidine; history of tendon disorders related to fluoroquinolone administration; pregnancy and breast-feeding (cartilage damage in animal studies).", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 250 mg, 500 mg, 750 mg; IV infusion: 200 mg/100 mL, 400 mg/200 mL; ophthalmic and otic drops 0.3%.", "monitoring": "ECG (QTc interval), renal function, blood glucose (dysglycemia risk in diabetics), surveillance for tendon pain or swelling."}

name: Vancomycin
description: {"atc": "J01XA01", "indications": "Severe Gram-positive infections caused by Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA): bacteremia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, hospital-acquired pneumonia. Oral formulation strictly indicated for Clostridioides difficile colitis. WHO EML Watch Group.", "mechanism": "Glycopeptide: binds the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of cell wall peptidoglycan precursors, sterically blocking transglycosylase and transpeptidase enzymes from cross-linking the peptidoglycan wall. Bactericidal.", "pharmacokinetics": "Zero oral absorption (oral route only acts intraluminally in C. difficile colitis); IV administration requires slow infusion; Excreted 80-90% unchanged by the kidneys; Half-life 4-6 hours (dramatically prolonged in renal impairment).", "pearls": "⚠️ Red Man Syndrome (Histamine Reaction): Rapid infusion (<60 min) causes non-IgE mast cell degranulation, triggering intense pruritic erythema and flushing of the face, neck, and upper torso, accompanied by hypotension and tachycardia (prevent by infusing <=1 g over at least 60 minutes or 10 mg/min). ⚠️ Nephrotoxicity: Increases significantly with trough levels >20 mcg/mL or when combined with piperacillin-tazobactam, aminoglycosides, or loop diuretics. Therapeutic Drug Monitoring target trough: 15-20 mcg/mL for serious MRSA infections (or AUC/MIC ratio 400-600).", "contraindications": "Known severe hypersensitivity to vancomycin.", "dosageForms": "Powder for injection: 500 mg, 1,000 mg vials; oral capsules: 125 mg, 250 mg.", "monitoring": "Serum trough concentration prior to 4th dose; serum creatinine and BUN; hearing screening in prolonged courses."}

name: Quinine
description: {"atc": "P01BC01", "indications": "Severe, complicated falciparum malaria (where IV artesunate is unavailable); second-line treatment of uncomplicated malaria; refractory nocturnal muscle cramps. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Cinchona alkaloid: concentrates in the acidic food vacuole of Plasmodium, complexing with toxic free heme and inhibiting its polymerization into insoluble hemozoin.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid oral and parenteral absorption; 70-90% protein bound; Extensively metabolized in the liver via CYP3A4; Half-life 11-18 hours; Renally excreted metabolites.", "pearls": "⚠️ Cinchonism: Constellation of dose-dependent symptoms: tinnitus, high-frequency hearing loss, dizziness, headache, blurred vision, nausea, and dysphoria. ⚠️ Profound Hypoglycemia: Stimulates pancreatic beta-cell sulfonylurea receptors, triggering massive insulin secretion (dangerously common in pregnant women with severe malaria; IV dextrose co-infusion and frequent blood glucose checks are mandatory!). ⚠️ Cardiovascular Toxicity: QTc prolongation and arrhythmias on rapid IV infusion (never give as rapid IV bolus; infuse over 4 hours with loading dose).", "contraindications": "Optic neuritis, tinnitus, myasthenia gravis, G6PD deficiency with known hemolysis, concurrent use of mefloquine.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 200 mg, 300 mg (sulfate); injectable ampoules: 300 mg/mL (dihydrochloride) in 2 mL ampoules for slow IV infusion in 5% dextrose.", "monitoring": "Capillary blood glucose every 4 hours, continuous cardiac rhythm/ECG, auditory checks."}

name: Lisinopril
description: {"atc": "C09AA03", "indications": "Essential hypertension; heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF); post-myocardial infarction (within 24 hrs to improve survival); diabetic nephropathy (delays progression of proteinuria). WHO EML Core Medicine.", "mechanism": "Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitor: competitively inhibits ACE (kininase II), blocking conversion of angiotensin I to the potent vasoconstrictor angiotensin II. Decreases aldosterone secretion, promotes natriuresis, and inhibits breakdown of bradykinin.", "pharmacokinetics": "Directly active molecule (NOT a prodrug, unlike enalapril/ramipril); Peak effect 6 hours; Long half-life of 12 hours (once-daily dosing); Excreted 100% unchanged in urine.", "pearls": "Mortality benefit in HFrEF and post-MI. Renal protective in diabetes by selectively dilating the efferent renal arteriole, reducing intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria. ⚠️ Dry Intractable Cough (~10-20%): Caused by accumulation of pulmonary bradykinin and substance P (switch to an ARB like Losartan). ⚠️ Hyperkalemia: Decreased aldosterone reduces renal K+ excretion (monitor K+ closely if combined with spironolactone). ⚠️ Angioedema: Life-threatening bradykinin-mediated airway swelling (more common in Black patients; absolute contraindication to re-exposure). ⚠️ Teratogenic: Fetopathy, renal agenesis, oligohydramnios.", "contraindications": "History of ACE-inhibitor-associated angioedema; hereditary or idiopathic angioedema; bilateral renal artery stenosis; pregnancy (2nd and 3rd trimesters); concurrent use of sacubitril (must observe 36-hr washout).", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg.", "monitoring": "Baseline and 1-2 week serum creatinine and potassium (up to 30% rise in creatinine is acceptable); blood pressure; monitor for cough and airway swelling."}

name: Amlodipine
description: {"atc": "C08CA01", "indications": "First-line antihypertensive agent (alone or in combination); chronic stable angina pectoris; vasospastic (Prinzmetal's) angina. WHO EML Core Medicine.", "mechanism": "Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (CCB): selectively inhibits L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle cells, preventing calcium influx and causing peripheral arterial vasodilation and reduction in systemic vascular resistance (SVR).", "pharmacokinetics": "Slow, sustained absorption (peak 6-12 hours); High oral bioavailability (60-80%); Elimination half-life 35-50 hours (enables true once-daily dosing with smooth 24-hour BP control); Hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4.", "pearls": "Does not cause reflex tachycardia due to its slow onset and prolonged clearance. ⚠️ Dependent Peripheral Ankle Edema: Common dose-dependent side effect caused by preferential precapillary arteriolar vasodilation increasing intracapillary hydrostatic pressure (not fluid overload!). Adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB causes postcapillary venodilation, normalizing capillary pressure and reducing edema. Safe in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction; does not depress cardiac contractility.", "contraindications": "Severe aortic stenosis; cardiogenic shock; unstable angina (except Prinzmetal's); severe hypotension.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg.", "monitoring": "Blood pressure, check for peripheral lower extremity edema, heart rate."}

name: Furosemide
description: {"atc": "C03CA01", "indications": "Acute pulmonary edema; chronic congestive heart failure with fluid overload; ascites in cirrhosis (combined with spironolactone); nephrotic syndrome; hypercalcemia. WHO EML Core Medicine.", "mechanism": "High-ceiling loop diuretic: reversibly inhibits the Na+/K+/2Cl- (NKCC2) cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, abolishing the hypertonic medullary gradient and causing profound excretion of sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium, calcium, and water.", "pharmacokinetics": "Oral bioavailability ~50% (oral to IV dose ratio is 2:1); Onset IV 5 minutes ('lasix = lasts six hours'), Oral 30-60 min; Duration 6-8 hrs; Half-life 1-1.5 hrs; Secreted into tubular lumen by organic acid transporters.", "pearls": "Most potent class of diuretics for symptomatic volume unloading in acute decompensated heart failure. IV administration produces immediate venodilation via renal prostaglandin release, relieving pulmonary congestion even before diuresis begins. ⚠️ Electrolyte Derangements: Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia (loops lose calcium, unlike thiazides), and contraction metabolic alkalosis. ⚠️ Ototoxicity: Tinnitus and sensorineural hearing loss, especially with rapid high-dose IV boluses (>4 mg/min) or co-administration of aminoglycosides. Hyperuricemia (can trigger acute gouty arthritis).", "contraindications": "Anuria unresponsive to test dose; severe hypokalemia; severe hyponatremia; hepatic encephalopathy; known hypersensitivity to sulfonamides.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 20 mg, 40 mg, 80 mg; oral solution 10 mg/mL; injectable solution: 10 mg/mL (20 mg in 2 mL, 250 mg in 25 mL ampoules).", "monitoring": "Daily weights, fluid balance, serum electrolytes (K+, Na+, Mg2+), serum creatinine and BUN, blood pressure, hearing."}

name: Lidocaine
description: {"atc": "N01BB02", "indications": "Local and regional infiltration anesthesia; peripheral nerve blocks; spinal and epidural anesthesia; topical mucosal anesthesia; systemic IV lidocaine infusion for perioperative analgesia; Class Ib antiarrhythmic for ventricular arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia/VF). WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Voltage-gated sodium channel blocker (Nav1.5, Nav1.7): reversibly binds the intracellular S6 segment of domain IV, blocking sodium influx and halting axonal action potential generation and propagation. Preferentially binds active/open and inactivated states (use-dependent block).", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid onset (2-5 min); Intermediate duration (60-120 min plain, extended to 240 min with epinephrine 1:200,000); Hepatic de-ethylation by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 to monoethylglycinexylidide (MEGX); Elimination half-life 1.5-2 hours; Maximum dose: 3-4.5 mg/kg plain, up to 7 mg/kg with epinephrine.", "pearls": "⚠️ Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST): Initial signs include circumoral numbness, metallic taste in mouth, tinnitus, dizziness, visual disturbances, progressing to muscle twitching, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and cardiovascular collapse (ventricular arrhythmias, asystole). Emergency antidote: 20% Lipid Emulsion (Intralipid: 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 1 min, followed by 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion). Addition of Epinephrine (adrenaline 1:200,000) causes local vasoconstriction, reducing systemic absorption, prolonging block duration, and providing a marker for accidental intravascular injection.", "contraindications": "Complete heart block, severe sinoatrial block; known allergy to amino-amides; application of epinephrine-containing solutions to end-artery anatomical areas (digits, penis, nose, ears - risk of ischemic necrosis).", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 0.5%, 1%, 2% (with and without Epinephrine 1:200,000); 4% topical solution; 5% ointment; 10% oral spray; 2.5% Lidocaine + 2.5% Prilocaine (EMLA cream).", "monitoring": "Continuous ECG during blocks, mental status check during injection, signs of LAST, blood pressure, local site assessment."}

name: Atropine
description: {"atc": "A03BA01", "indications": "Emergency treatment of severe symptomatic bradycardia and AV nodal heart block (ACLS algorithm); antidote for organophosphate, carbamate, and nerve agent poisoning; antisialagogue (reduction of airway secretions); co-administered with anticholinesterases. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Competitive, reversible antagonist of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (M1, M2, M3, M4, M5). Blocks vagal cardiac parasympathetic tone at M2 receptors in the SA and AV nodes, increasing sinus rate and AV conduction velocity.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset IV 1-2 minutes; Duration of vagolytic effect 1-2 hours; Hepatic metabolism ~50%; Renal excretion ~30-50% unchanged; Crosses blood-brain barrier and placenta.", "pearls": "⚠️ Paradoxical bradycardia occurs with low doses (<0.5 mg IV) due to central vagal stimulation or blockade of presynaptic inhibitory M1 receptors on postganglionic parasympathetic nerves (always give >=0.5 mg in adults). High doses cause classic 'anticholinergic toxidrome': 'Blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, red as a beet, hot as a hare, dry as a bone' (mydriasis, delirium, cutaneous flushing, hyperthermia, dry mouth/skin, urinary retention). In organophosphate poisoning, titrate until pulmonary secretions are clear and bronchospasm resolves.", "contraindications": "Acute narrow-angle glaucoma; obstructive uropathy (prostatic hypertrophy); mechanical gastrointestinal obstruction, paralytic ileus, severe ulcerative colitis/toxic megacolon; myasthenia gravis (unless used to treat cholinergic crisis).", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 0.5 mg/mL, 0.6 mg/mL, and 1 mg/mL ampoules.", "monitoring": "Continuous ECG/heart rate, pupillary diameter, body temperature, airway secretion dryness, bladder palpation."}

name: Atorvastatin
description: {"atc": "C10AA05", "indications": "Primary and secondary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), myocardial infarction, and stroke; hypercholesterolemia; familial hypercholesterolemia. name: Acetylsalicylic acid
description: {"atc": "N02BA01", "indications": "Low-dose (75-150 mg): Secondary prevention of cardiovascular events (acute coronary syndromes, post-PCI, ischemic stroke, TIA); High-dose (300-1,000 mg): Mild-to-moderate inflammatory pain, acute migraine, rheumatic fever, Kawasaki disease. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Irreversible acetylation of serine 529 in COX-1 and serine 516 in COX-2. Irreversibly inhibits platelet thromboxane A2 (TXA2) synthesis for the entire lifespan of the platelet (7-10 days), blocking platelet aggregation.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapidly absorbed in stomach and upper small intestine; Hydrolyzed by plasma and tissue esterases to salicylic acid (half-life 15-20 min); Salicylate half-life is dose-dependent (2-3 hrs at low dose, up to 15-30 hrs at toxic anti-inflammatory doses due to hepatic clearance saturation); Renal excretion.", "pearls": "⚠️ Reye's Syndrome: Strictly contraindicated in children and adolescents under 16 years with viral illnesses (varicella, influenza) due to risk of microvesicular fatty liver disease and encephalopathy (exception: Kawasaki disease). ⚠️ Samter's Triad (Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease / AERD): Asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, and bronchospasm upon COX-1 inhibition (shunt to 5-lipoxygenase pathway and leukotriene synthesis). ⚠️ Salicylate Poisoning: Tinnitus, respiratory alkalosis (direct medullary center stimulation) followed by high anion gap metabolic acidosis (uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation); treat with urine alkalinization (IV NaHCO3) and hemodialysis.", "contraindications": "Children <16 years with viral infection; active peptic ulceration; hemophilia/bleeding disorders; severe renal/hepatic failure; 3rd trimester pregnancy; history of AERD.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 75 mg, 81 mg, 100 mg (enteric-coated cardio-aspirin); 300 mg, 500 mg soluble/effervescent tablets.", "monitoring": "Stool occult blood, bleeding time/platelet count, renal function, serum salicylate level in toxicity."}

name: Salbutamol
description: {"atc": "R03AC02", "indications": "Rapid relief of acute bronchospasm in bronchial asthma, COPD exacerbation, exercise-induced asthma; hyperkalemia emergency treatment (shifts K+ into cells). WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Short-Acting Beta-2 Adrenergic Agonist (SABA): selectively stimulates beta-2 adrenoceptors on bronchial smooth muscle, activating adenylyl cyclase, increasing intracellular cAMP, activating PKA, and causing rapid bronchodilation.", "pharmacokinetics": "Inhaled onset: 2-5 minutes; Peak effect: 15-30 minutes; Duration: 4-6 hours; Hepatic sulfation to inactive metabolites; Renal elimination.", "pearls": "Universal first-line rescue bronchodilator. Paradoxical overuse (>2 canisters per month) indicates poorly controlled asthma and increases mortality; always combine with Inhaled Corticosteroid (ICS) controller therapy. High systemic doses cause beta-2 mediated potassium shift into skeletal muscle (IV or high nebulizer doses used as temporary temporizing measure in severe hyperkalemia). Side effects: fine skeletal muscle tremor (finger tremor via beta-2 receptors in muscle spindles), tachycardia (beta-1 cross-reactivity and reflex response to peripheral vasodilation), and transient hypokalemia.", "contraindications": "Hypersensitivity to salbutamol. Tocolytic use contraindicated in antepartum hemorrhage, pre-eclampsia, or intrauterine fetal demise.", "dosageForms": "Metered Dose Inhaler (MDI): 100 mcg/actuation; dry powder inhaler; nebulizer solution: 2.5 mg/2.5 mL, 5 mg/2.5 mL; oral syrup 2 mg/5 mL; IV infusion.", "monitoring": "Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR), respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate, serum potassium if high-dose nebulization."}

name: Fluticasone

WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Potent synthetic glucocorticoid: diffuses into cells, binds the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor, translocates to the nucleus, and represses transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-4, IL-5, TNF-alpha) while upregulating anti-inflammatory lipocortin-1, downregulating airway eosinophils, mast cells, and mucosal edema.", "pharmacokinetics": "Extremely low oral systemic bioavailability (<1% due to near-complete first-pass hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4); Inhaled lung fraction acts locally before hepatic clearance; Half-life 8-11 hours.", "pearls": "Cornerstone of modern asthma maintenance therapy: treats the underlying chronic mucosal inflammation rather than just smooth muscle contraction. ⚠️ Local Adverse Effects: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) and dysphonia/hoarseness due to laryngeal myopathy (instruct patient to use a spacer device and ALWAYS rinse mouth with water and spit after each inhalation). name: Codeine
description: {"atc": "N02AA59", "indications": "Mild to moderate pain (Step 2 on WHO Pain Ladder, often combined with Paracetamol); cough suppression (antitussive). WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Weak opioid prodrug. Has low intrinsic affinity for mu-opioid receptors; ~10% is converted into active morphine by hepatic cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6).", "pharmacokinetics": "Good oral bioavailability (~50%); Half-life 2.5-3 hours; Renal excretion of glucuronides and free morphine.", "pearls": "⚠️ CYP2D6 Pharmacogenomic Danger: 'Ultra-rapid metabolizers' (duplication of CYP2D6 gene, up to 10-29% in North African and Middle Eastern populations) rapidly convert codeine to lethal toxic levels of morphine (cases of fatal pediatric respiratory arrest post-tonsillectomy and maternal-infant toxicity via breast milk). 'Poor metabolizers' (~7-10% of Caucasians) lack CYP2D6 activity and experience zero analgesic benefit. Black box warning: strictly contraindicated in children <12 years and post-tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy in patients <18 years.", "contraindications": "Children <12 years; post-tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy in children <18 years; nursing mothers; known ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolizers; severe respiratory insufficiency.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 15 mg, 30 mg, 60 mg; Codeine + Paracetamol combination (30/500 mg Co-codamol); cough syrup 15 mg/5 mL.", "monitoring": "Respiratory rate, signs of opioid toxicity, bowel movements."}

name: Omeprazole
description: {"atc": "A02BC01", "indications": "Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), erosive esophagitis, gastric and duodenal peptic ulcers, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, H. pylori eradication, prophylaxis of NSAID-induced ulcers. WHO EML Core Medicine.", "mechanism": "Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI): prodrug that crosses parietal cell membranes, gets trapped in the acidic secretory canaliculi, undergoes acid-catalyzed conversion to active sulfonamide, and forms an irreversible covalent disulfide bond with the H+/K+-ATPase enzyme, profoundly shutting down gastric acid secretion.", "pharmacokinetics": "Delayed-release enteric coating protects against gastric acid degradation; Rapidly absorbed in duodenum; Peak plasma level 2 hours; Elimination half-life ~1 hour, but duration of acid inhibition lasts 24-48 hours until new proton pump enzymes are synthesized; Hepatic metabolism via CYP2C19.", "pearls": "Take 30-60 minutes BEFORE breakfast: proton pumps are most active and sensitive to inhibition upon morning meal stimulation. Chronic long-term PPI therapy causes hypochlorhydria, associated with decreased intestinal absorption of calcium and magnesium (increased hip fracture risk), Vitamin B12 deficiency, increased risk of Clostridioides difficile colitis, and microscopic colitis. ⚠️ Drug Interaction: Inhibits CYP2C19, decreasing bioactivation of clopidogrel (pantoprazole has less CYP2C19 interaction).", "contraindications": "Hypersensitivity to substituted benzimidazoles; concurrent administration with rilpivirine or nelfinavir.", "dosageForms": "Enteric-coated capsules/tablets: 10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg; powder for IV injection: 40 mg vials.", "monitoring": "Symptom resolution, magnesium levels in long-term therapy (>1 yr), C. difficile symptoms, bone density in elderly."}

name: Ondansetron
description: {"atc": "A04AA01", "indications": "Prevention and treatment of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV); radiation-induced emesis; postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV); acute gastroenteritis emesis in pediatrics. name: Diazepam
description: {"atc": "N05BA01", "indications": "Status epilepticus rescue; acute anxiety states; alcohol withdrawal syndrome (delirium tremens prophylaxis); muscle spasm; perioperative sedation. WHO EML Core Medicine.", "mechanism": "Long-acting benzodiazepine: binds gamma-2 subunit of GABA-A receptors, increasing channel opening frequency and enhancing central inhibitory GABAergic neurotransmission across the limbic system, thalamus, and motor cortex.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid oral absorption; Highly lipophilic with rapid entry into brain; Prolonged duration due to hepatic CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 metabolism to active long-lived metabolites: desmethyldiazepam (half-life up to 100 hrs), temazepam, and oxazepam; High risk of accumulation with repeated dosing in the elderly.", "pearls": "First-line emergency termination of status epilepticus (IV 10 mg or rectal gel 10-20 mg if IV access is unavailable; now often substituted by IV Lorazepam due to longer anticonvulsant duration). Drug of choice for alcohol withdrawal (CIWA protocol) due to smooth self-tapering via long-acting active metabolites. ⚠️ Respiratory depression and hypotension when combined with opioids. Tolerance, physical dependence, and severe withdrawal seizures on abrupt cessation after chronic use.", "contraindications": "Severe respiratory insufficiency; severe sleep apnea syndrome; myasthenia gravis; acute narrow-angle glaucoma; severe hepatic insufficiency.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 2 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg; oral solution; injectable solution: 5 mg/mL (10 mg in 2 mL ampoules); rectal tubes/gel: 5 mg, 10 mg.", "monitoring": "Respiratory rate, pulse oximetry, sedation depth, signs of benzodiazepine withdrawal on discontinuation."}
