name: Haloperidol
description: {"atc": "N05AD01", "indications": "Acute psychotic agitation; schizophrenia; acute delirium in intensive care; severe Tourette syndrome and chorea; refractory palliative nausea. WHO EML Core Medicine.", "mechanism": "High-potency first-generation butyrophenone antipsychotic: potent selective antagonist of postsynaptic dopamine D2 receptors in the mesolimbic and mesocortical systems.", "pharmacokinetics": "Peak plasma level: oral 2-6 hrs, IM 20 min; Half-life 15-30 hours; Extensive hepatic metabolism via glucuronidation and CYP3A4/CYP2D6; Highly lipophilic.", "pearls": "Potent antipsychotic with minimal anticholinergic, antihistaminic, or alpha-adrenergic side effects (rarely causes hypotension, sedation, or weight gain). ⚠️ Extrapyramidal Symptoms (EPS): High risk due to potent D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway: acute dystonic reactions (torticollis, oculogyric crisis; treat with IV benztropine/diphenhydramine), akathisia (motor restlessness), and pseudoparkinsonism. ⚠️ Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS): Rare life-threatening tetrad of hyperthermia, 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity, autonomic instability, and altered mental status with high serum CK (treat with Dantrolene and Bromocriptine). ⚠️ QTc prolongation and Torsades de Pointes on IV administration.", "contraindications": "Parkinson's disease; dementia with Lewy bodies; severe CNS depression or comatose states; baseline prolonged QTc interval.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 0.5 mg, 1.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg; oral drops 2 mg/mL; injectable: 5 mg/mL ampoules; depot intramuscular decanoate: 50 mg/mL, 100 mg/mL.", "monitoring": "ECG (QTc interval, especially if given IV), neurological assessment for involuntary movements (AIMS scale), core temperature."}

name: Diazepam
description: {"atc": "N05BA01", "indications": "Status epilepticus rescue; acute anxiety states; alcohol withdrawal syndrome (delirium tremens prophylaxis); muscle spasm; perioperative sedation. WHO EML Core Medicine.", "mechanism": "Long-acting benzodiazepine: binds gamma-2 subunit of GABA-A receptors, increasing channel opening frequency and enhancing central inhibitory GABAergic neurotransmission across the limbic system, thalamus, and motor cortex.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid oral absorption; Highly lipophilic with rapid entry into brain; Prolonged duration due to hepatic CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 metabolism to active long-lived metabolites: desmethyldiazepam (half-life up to 100 hrs), temazepam, and oxazepam; High risk of accumulation with repeated dosing in the elderly.", "pearls": "First-line emergency termination of status epilepticus (IV 10 mg or rectal gel 10-20 mg if IV access is unavailable; now often substituted by IV Lorazepam due to longer anticonvulsant duration). Drug of choice for alcohol withdrawal (CIWA protocol) due to smooth self-tapering via long-acting active metabolites. ⚠️ Respiratory depression and hypotension when combined with opioids. Tolerance, physical dependence, and severe withdrawal seizures on abrupt cessation after chronic use.", "contraindications": "Severe respiratory insufficiency; severe sleep apnea syndrome; myasthenia gravis; acute narrow-angle glaucoma; severe hepatic insufficiency.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 2 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg; oral solution; injectable solution: 5 mg/mL (10 mg in 2 mL ampoules); rectal tubes/gel: 5 mg, 10 mg.", "monitoring": "Respiratory rate, pulse oximetry, sedation depth, signs of benzodiazepine withdrawal on discontinuation."}

name: Midazolam
description: {"atc": "N01CD08", "indications": "Preoperative anxiolysis and anterograde amnesia; procedural sedation; induction of anesthesia (high dose); continuous sedation in intensive care; status epilepticus rescue. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors, increasing channel opening frequency in the limbic system, cortex, and thalamus.", "pharmacokinetics": "Water-soluble at acidic pH (ampoule pH 3.5), lipid-soluble at physiological pH (pH 7.4), allowing rapid crossing of the blood-brain barrier. Synergistic respiratory depression when combined with opioids. Reversible with the competitive antagonist Flumazenil (0.2 mg IV titrated, beware resedation due to shorter half-life of flumazenil ~1 hour). name: Metformin
description: {"atc": "A10BA02", "indications": "First-line oral pharmacotherapy for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus; Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS); gestational diabetes where insulin is unavailable. WHO EML Core Medicine.", "mechanism": "Biguanide: activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) in hepatocytes, suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis; increases peripheral insulin sensitivity in skeletal muscle and reduces intestinal glucose absorption.", "pharmacokinetics": "Oral bioavailability 50-60%; Does NOT bind plasma proteins; Negligible hepatic metabolism; Excreted 100% unchanged in urine via organic cation transporters (OCT2); Elimination half-life ~6.5 hours.", "pearls": "Does NOT cause hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy (euglycemic agent) and promotes modest weight loss. Cardiovascular protection in overweight T2DM patients. High incidence of transient GI side effects (nausea, abdominal bloating, metallic taste, osmotic diarrhea; minimize by taking with food and slow titration). Long-term use impairs ileal absorption of Vitamin B12. ⚠️ Lactic Acidosis (MALA): Rare but high mortality (~30-50%); drug accumulates when renal clearance falls. Rule of thumb: reduce dose by 50% if eGFR 30-45 mL/min; discontinue immediately if eGFR <30 mL/min or in acute hypoxemia/shock. Hold 48 hours before and after IV iodinated radiocontrast procedures.", "contraindications": "Severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min); acute conditions predisposing to tissue hypoxia (cardiogenic shock, acute MI, decompensated heart failure, sepsis, severe respiratory failure); acute metabolic acidosis.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 500 mg, 850 mg, 1000 mg; extended-release (XR) tablets: 500 mg, 750 mg, 1000 mg.", "monitoring": "eGFR and serum creatinine every 3-6 months; HbA1c; serum Vitamin B12 levels every 1-2 years."}

description: {"atc": "H03AA01", "indications": "Primary, secondary, and tertiary hypothyroidism; congenital hypothyroidism; myxedema coma; TSH suppression therapy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma. name: Oxytocin
description: {"atc": "H01BB02", "indications": "First-line agent for Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL) to prevent postpartum hemorrhage (PPH); treatment of uterine atony and PPH; induction and augmentation of labor. WHO EML Core Medicine.", "mechanism": "Synthetic nonapeptide identical to posterior pituitary oxytocin. Binds Gq-coupled oxytocin receptors on uterine myometrium, activating the phospholipase C-IP3 pathway and increasing intracellular calcium, stimulating rhythmic uterine contractions.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset: IV immediate, IM 3-5 minutes; Clinical duration 30-60 minutes; Rapidly degraded by placental oxytocinase in plasma; Elimination half-life 3-5 minutes (enables instantaneous titratability via infusion).", "pearls": "Single most effective agent for preventing postpartum hemorrhage (administer 10 IU IM or slow IV immediately upon delivery of anterior shoulder/baby). ⚠️ Rapid IV Bolus Danger: Rapid undiluted IV push causes transient marked hypotension, reflex tachycardia, and coronary vasoconstriction (always administer by slow IV injection over 1-2 minutes or dilute in crystalloid infusion). ⚠️ Water Intoxication: Oxytocin has structural homology to vasopressin (ADH); prolonged high-dose infusions with hypotonic fluids (e.g. 5% Dextrose) can produce severe hyponatremic encephalopathy, seizures, and coma.", "contraindications": "Hypertonic or obstructed uterine contractions; cephalopelvic disproportion; fetal distress before delivery; placenta previa; previous classical uterine cesarean section.", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 10 IU in 1 mL ampoules (requires cold-chain storage 2-8°C).", "monitoring": "Uterine tone/contraction frequency and strength, continuous fetal heart rate during labor, maternal blood pressure and pulse, fluid balance."}

name: Oxytocin
description: {"atc": "H01BB02", "indications": "First-line agent for Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL) to prevent postpartum hemorrhage (PPH); treatment of uterine atony and PPH; induction and augmentation of labor. WHO EML Core Medicine.", "mechanism": "Synthetic nonapeptide identical to posterior pituitary oxytocin. Binds Gq-coupled oxytocin receptors on uterine myometrium, activating the phospholipase C-IP3 pathway and increasing intracellular calcium, stimulating rhythmic uterine contractions.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset: IV immediate, IM 3-5 minutes; Clinical duration 30-60 minutes; Rapidly degraded by placental oxytocinase in plasma; Elimination half-life 3-5 minutes (enables instantaneous titratability via infusion).", "pearls": "Single most effective agent for preventing postpartum hemorrhage (administer 10 IU IM or slow IV immediately upon delivery of anterior shoulder/baby). ⚠️ Rapid IV Bolus Danger: Rapid undiluted IV push causes transient marked hypotension, reflex tachycardia, and coronary vasoconstriction (always administer by slow IV injection over 1-2 minutes or dilute in crystalloid infusion). ⚠️ Water Intoxication: Oxytocin has structural homology to vasopressin (ADH); prolonged high-dose infusions with hypotonic fluids (e.g. 5% Dextrose) can produce severe hyponatremic encephalopathy, seizures, and coma.", "contraindications": "Hypertonic or obstructed uterine contractions; cephalopelvic disproportion; fetal distress before delivery; placenta previa; previous classical uterine cesarean section.", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 10 IU in 1 mL ampoules (requires cold-chain storage 2-8°C).", "monitoring": "Uterine tone/contraction frequency and strength, continuous fetal heart rate during labor, maternal blood pressure and pulse, fluid balance."}

name: Salbutamol
description: {"atc": "R03AC02", "indications": "Rapid relief of acute bronchospasm in bronchial asthma, COPD exacerbation, exercise-induced asthma; hyperkalemia emergency treatment (shifts K+ into cells). WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Short-Acting Beta-2 Adrenergic Agonist (SABA): selectively stimulates beta-2 adrenoceptors on bronchial smooth muscle, activating adenylyl cyclase, increasing intracellular cAMP, activating PKA, and causing rapid bronchodilation.", "pharmacokinetics": "Inhaled onset: 2-5 minutes; Peak effect: 15-30 minutes; Duration: 4-6 hours; Hepatic sulfation to inactive metabolites; Renal elimination.", "pearls": "Universal first-line rescue bronchodilator. Paradoxical overuse (>2 canisters per month) indicates poorly controlled asthma and increases mortality; always combine with Inhaled Corticosteroid (ICS) controller therapy. High systemic doses cause beta-2 mediated potassium shift into skeletal muscle (IV or high nebulizer doses used as temporary temporizing measure in severe hyperkalemia). Side effects: fine skeletal muscle tremor (finger tremor via beta-2 receptors in muscle spindles), tachycardia (beta-1 cross-reactivity and reflex response to peripheral vasodilation), and transient hypokalemia.", "contraindications": "Hypersensitivity to salbutamol. Tocolytic use contraindicated in antepartum hemorrhage, pre-eclampsia, or intrauterine fetal demise.", "dosageForms": "Metered Dose Inhaler (MDI): 100 mcg/actuation; dry powder inhaler; nebulizer solution: 2.5 mg/2.5 mL, 5 mg/2.5 mL; oral syrup 2 mg/5 mL; IV infusion.", "monitoring": "Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR), respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate, serum potassium if high-dose nebulization."}

name: Ibuprofen
description: {"atc": "M01AE01", "indications": "Mild to moderate pain, dysmenorrhea, dental pain, headache; musculoskeletal inflammation (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis); closure of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in preterm neonates; fever reduction. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Reversible, competitive non-selective inhibitor of both cyclo-oxygenase-1 (COX-1) and cyclo-oxygenase-2 (COX-2), decreasing peripheral and central prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) synthesis.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid absorption (peak plasma concentration 1-2 hours); 99% plasma protein bound; Hepatic CYP2C9 and CYP2C8 metabolism; Elimination half-life 1.8-2.0 hours; Renal excretion of metabolites.", "pearls": "Generally regarded as the non-selective NSAID with the lowest gastrointestinal toxicity profile at standard over-the-counter doses (<=1,200 mg/day). Reversibly inhibits platelet aggregation (antiplatelet effect ends when drug is cleared, unlike aspirin). Can competitively interfere with the cardioprotective antiplatelet effect of aspirin (take aspirin 30 min before ibuprofen). ⚠️ Renal Papillary Necrosis & Triple Whammy: Combination of NSAID (afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction via prostaglandin block) + ACE inhibitor/ARB (efferent arteriolar vasodilation) + Diuretic causes acute prerenal kidney failure.", "contraindications": "Active gastrointestinal bleeding or peptic ulcer disease; severe congestive heart failure (NYHA III-IV); severe renal impairment; third trimester of pregnancy (premature closure of fetal ductus arteriosus).", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets/capsules: 200 mg, 400 mg, 600 mg, 800 mg; oral suspension: 100 mg/5 mL; topical gel 5%; IV infusion (for PDA closure / acute pain).", "monitoring": "Blood pressure (can elevate BP by 3-5 mmHg), serum creatinine and eGFR, GI symptom review, complete blood count."}

name: Fluticasone
description: {"atc": "R03BA05", "indications": "Maintenance anti-inflammatory treatment of persistent asthma; moderate-to-severe COPD (combined with LABA); allergic rhinitis (intranasal). WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Potent synthetic glucocorticoid: diffuses into cells, binds the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor, translocates to the nucleus, and represses transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-4, IL-5, TNF-alpha) while upregulating anti-inflammatory lipocortin-1, downregulating airway eosinophils, mast cells, and mucosal edema.", "pharmacokinetics": "Extremely low oral systemic bioavailability (<1% due to near-complete first-pass hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4); Inhaled lung fraction acts locally before hepatic clearance; Half-life 8-11 hours.", "pearls": "Cornerstone of modern asthma maintenance therapy: treats the underlying chronic mucosal inflammation rather than just smooth muscle contraction. ⚠️ Local Adverse Effects: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) and dysphonia/hoarseness due to laryngeal myopathy (instruct patient to use a spacer device and ALWAYS rinse mouth with water and spit after each inhalation). High long-term doses can cause systemic effects (mild hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression, reduced bone mineral density, bruising).", "contraindications": "Primary treatment of status asthmaticus or acute bronchospasm where rapid bronchodilation is needed; untreated fungal, bacterial, or tubercular infections of the respiratory tract.", "dosageForms": "Inhalation aerosol (MDI): 50, 125, 250 mcg/actuation; Dry powder inhaler (Accuhaler); nasal spray 50 mcg/actuation.", "monitoring": "Asthma Control Test (ACT), visual inspection of oral cavity for candidiasis, pediatric growth velocity."}

name: Gentamicin
description: {"atc": "J01GB03", "indications": "Severe Gram-negative aerobic bacillary infections (Pseudomonas, Enterobacteriaceae); synergistic combination with ampicillin for enterococcal/streptococcal infective endocarditis; neonatal sepsis. WHO EML Access Group.", "mechanism": "Aminoglycoside: irreversibly binds the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA genetic code and premature termination of protein synthesis. Highly bactericidal with concentration-dependent killing and prolonged post-antibiotic effect (PAE).", "pharmacokinetics": "Polar polycationic molecule: essentially zero oral absorption (requires IV/IM); Poor intracellular and CSF penetration; Excreted 100% unchanged via glomerular filtration; Half-life 2-3 hours (dramatically prolonged in renal failure).", "pearls": "Concentration-dependent killing: once-daily extended-interval dosing (5-7 mg/kg/day) maximizes peak-to-MIC ratio (>8-10) while allowing trough concentrations to drop <1 mcg/mL, minimizing toxicity. ⚠️ Ototoxicity (vestibular > cochlear damage): Irreversible destruction of sensory hair cells via free radical generation (accumulates in endolymph). ⚠️ Nephrotoxicity: Reversible non-oliguric acute kidney injury due to uptake into proximal tubular cells (megalin/cubilin receptor-mediated). Curare-like neuromuscular blockade: inhibits presynaptic acetylcholine release (contraindicated in Myasthenia Gravis).", "contraindications": "Myasthenia gravis; pre-existing severe vestibulocochlear damage; concurrent use of other potent ototoxic/nephrotoxic drugs (furosemide, cisplatin).", "dosageForms": "Solution for injection: 40 mg/mL (80 mg in 2 mL ampoules); ophthalmic drops 0.3%.", "monitoring": "Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM): trough level <1 mcg/mL (immediately prior to next dose) to prevent toxicity; peak level 15-20 mcg/mL; serum creatinine twice weekly; vestibular/hearing assessment."}

name: Ciprofloxacin
description: {"atc": "J01MA02", "indications": "Complicated urinary tract infections, pyelonephritis, bacterial prostatitis, traveler's diarrhea (shigellosis, salmonellosis), intra-abdominal infections, pulmonary Pseudomonas in cystic fibrosis, anthrax prophylaxis. WHO EML Watch Group.", "mechanism": "Fluoroquinolone: bactericidal inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, preventing DNA supercoiling, transcription, and replication.", "pharmacokinetics": "Excellent oral bioavailability (70-80%); Large volume of distribution; Moderate hepatic metabolism; Elimination predominantly renal; Half-life 4 hours.", "pearls": "Oral route provides tissue levels comparable to IV administration. Chelation interaction: Polyvalent cations (calcium, iron, aluminum, magnesium antacids) reduce oral absorption by >90% (space by >=2 hours). ⚠️ Tendinitis & Tendon Rupture (especially Achilles tendon): Risk highest in elderly patients and those taking systemic corticosteroids. ⚠️ Prolongation of QT Interval: Increases risk of Torsades de Pointes. ⚠️ Neuropsychiatric Effects & Aortic Dissection warnings: Can trigger seizures, confusion, hallucinations, and peripheral neuropathy.", "contraindications": "Concurrent use of tizanidine; history of tendon disorders related to fluoroquinolone administration; pregnancy and breast-feeding (cartilage damage in animal studies).", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 250 mg, 500 mg, 750 mg; IV infusion: 200 mg/100 mL, 400 mg/200 mL; ophthalmic and otic drops 0.3%.", "monitoring": "ECG (QTc interval), renal function, blood glucose (dysglycemia risk in diabetics), surveillance for tendon pain or swelling."}

name: Gentamicin
description: {"atc": "J01GB03", "indications": "Severe Gram-negative aerobic bacillary infections (Pseudomonas, Enterobacteriaceae); synergistic combination with ampicillin for enterococcal/streptococcal infective endocarditis; neonatal sepsis. WHO EML Access Group.", "mechanism": "Aminoglycoside: irreversibly binds the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA genetic code and premature termination of protein synthesis. Highly bactericidal with concentration-dependent killing and prolonged post-antibiotic effect (PAE).", "pharmacokinetics": "Polar polycationic molecule: essentially zero oral absorption (requires IV/IM); Poor intracellular and CSF penetration; Excreted 100% unchanged via glomerular filtration; Half-life 2-3 hours (dramatically prolonged in renal failure).", "pearls": "Concentration-dependent killing: once-daily extended-interval dosing (5-7 mg/kg/day) maximizes peak-to-MIC ratio (>8-10) while allowing trough concentrations to drop <1 mcg/mL, minimizing toxicity. ⚠️ Ototoxicity (vestibular > cochlear damage): Irreversible destruction of sensory hair cells via free radical generation (accumulates in endolymph). ⚠️ Nephrotoxicity: Reversible non-oliguric acute kidney injury due to uptake into proximal tubular cells (megalin/cubilin receptor-mediated). Curare-like neuromuscular blockade: inhibits presynaptic acetylcholine release (contraindicated in Myasthenia Gravis).", "contraindications": "Myasthenia gravis; pre-existing severe vestibulocochlear damage; concurrent use of other potent ototoxic/nephrotoxic drugs (furosemide, cisplatin).", "dosageForms": "Solution for injection: 40 mg/mL (80 mg in 2 mL ampoules); ophthalmic drops 0.3%.", "monitoring": "Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM): trough level <1 mcg/mL (immediately prior to next dose) to prevent toxicity; peak level 15-20 mcg/mL; serum creatinine twice weekly; vestibular/hearing assessment."}

name: Azithromycin
description: {"atc": "J01FA10", "indications": "Atypical community-acquired pneumonia (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella); Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis/cervicitis (1 g single dose); pertussis; trachoma elimination programs; MAC prophylaxis in HIV. WHO EML Watch Group.", "mechanism": "Azalide macrolide: reversibly binds the 50S ribosomal subunit at the 23S rRNA, inhibiting peptidyltransferase activity and transpeptidation during bacterial protein synthesis. Bacteriostatic.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid tissue uptake with tissue concentrations up to 50-fold higher than serum; Very long terminal half-life of 68 hours (enables once-daily dosing for 3-5 days); Biliary excretion.", "pearls": "Unlike erythromycin and clarithromycin, azithromycin does NOT inhibit hepatic CYP3A4, resulting in significantly fewer drug-drug interactions with statins, carbamazepine, and warfarin. Post-antibiotic effect extends therapeutic tissue levels for 4-5 days after the last dose. ⚠️ Cardiovascular Safety: Causes QT prolongation and has been associated with small increased risk of fatal cardiac arrhythmias in patients with underlying cardiac pathology.", "contraindications": "Known hypersensitivity to macrolides; history of cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction with prior azithromycin use.", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets/capsules: 250 mg, 500 mg; oral suspension: 200 mg/5 mL; powder for IV infusion: 500 mg.", "monitoring": "Baseline ECG in cardiac patients (QTc monitoring), liver function tests, hearing checks in high-dose prolonged therapy."}

name: Diclofenac
description: {"atc": "M01AB05", "indications": "Acute postoperative pain; renal colic (first-line in emergency settings); acute migraine; flare-ups of osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis; topical therapy for localized joint pain. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Preferential inhibition of COX-2 over COX-1; suppresses prostaglandin synthesis and reduces leukocyte intracellular arachidonic acid concentrations.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid absorption; Undergoes ~50% first-pass hepatic metabolism; Short elimination half-life 1-2 hours, but accumulates in synovial fluid where concentrations remain high for >11 hours; Hepatic CYP2C9 metabolism.", "pearls": "Exceptional efficacy in renal colic (relieves ureteric smooth muscle spasm and decreases renal capsular pressure by reducing afferent renal blood flow). ⚠️ Highest cardiovascular thrombotic risk among standard non-selective NSAIDs (similar risk profile to selective COX-2 inhibitors; avoid in patients with ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, and cerebrovascular disease). High incidence of transient elevation in hepatic transaminases (ALT/AST). Topical gel formulations achieve high synovial levels with <10% systemic absorption.", "contraindications": "Ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, history of stroke/TIA, congestive heart failure (NYHA II-IV); active GI ulcer/bleeding; severe hepatic/renal impairment.", "dosageForms": "Enteric-coated tablets: 25 mg, 50 mg; sustained release: 75 mg, 100 mg; ampoules for IM/IV injection: 75 mg in 3 mL; topical gel 1% and 2.32%; eye drops 0.1%.", "monitoring": "Baseline and periodic liver function tests (LFTs), blood pressure, serum creatinine, cardiovascular risk assessment."}

name: Ketorolac
description: {"atc": "M01AB15", "indications": "Short-term management (MAXIMUM 5 consecutive days) of moderate-to-severe acute postoperative and trauma pain; acute renal colic; ophthalmic drops for seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and post-cataract inflammation.", "mechanism": "Potent non-selective COX-1 and COX-2 inhibitor with marked analgesic potency comparable to low-to-moderate dose opioids, without sedative or respiratory depressant effects.", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid onset IV/IM 10-30 min; Peak effect 1-2 hours; Duration 4-6 hours; Elimination half-life 4-6 hours; 99% protein bound; Excreted primarily unchanged by kidneys.", "pearls": "⚠️ Severe Black Box Warning: STRICT 5-DAY MAXIMUM TREATMENT DURATION across all routes combined. High incidence of life-threatening gastrointestinal perforation, peptic ulceration, operative site bleeding (due to potent COX-1 inhibition of platelet TXA2), and acute renal failure. Never give preoperatively when hemostasis is critical. Dose must be reduced by 50% in patients >=65 years, weighing <50 kg, or with mildly elevated serum creatinine.", "contraindications": "Active or history of GI bleeding/perforation; advanced renal impairment or at risk for renal failure; suspected cerebrovascular bleeding; epidural or intrathecal administration; labor and delivery; combination with other NSAIDs.", "dosageForms": "Injectable: 10 mg/mL, 15 mg/mL, 30 mg/mL in 1 mL ampoules; oral tablets 10 mg (only for continuation of parenteral therapy); ophthalmic solution 0.5%.", "monitoring": "Strict count of treatment days (never exceed 5), urine output, serum BUN/creatinine, surgical drain volume, hemoglobin/hematocrit."}

name: Atropine
description: {"atc": "A03BA01", "indications": "Emergency treatment of severe symptomatic bradycardia and AV nodal heart block (ACLS algorithm); antidote for organophosphate, carbamate, and nerve agent poisoning; antisialagogue (reduction of airway secretions); co-administered with anticholinesterases. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Competitive, reversible antagonist of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (M1, M2, M3, M4, M5). Blocks vagal cardiac parasympathetic tone at M2 receptors in the SA and AV nodes, increasing sinus rate and AV conduction velocity.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset IV 1-2 minutes; Duration of vagolytic effect 1-2 hours; Hepatic metabolism ~50%; Renal excretion ~30-50% unchanged; Crosses blood-brain barrier and placenta.", "pearls": "⚠️ Paradoxical bradycardia occurs with low doses (<0.5 mg IV) due to central vagal stimulation or blockade of presynaptic inhibitory M1 receptors on postganglionic parasympathetic nerves (always give >=0.5 mg in adults). High doses cause classic 'anticholinergic toxidrome': 'Blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, red as a beet, hot as a hare, dry as a bone' (mydriasis, delirium, cutaneous flushing, hyperthermia, dry mouth/skin, urinary retention). In organophosphate poisoning, titrate until pulmonary secretions are clear and bronchospasm resolves.", "contraindications": "Acute narrow-angle glaucoma; obstructive uropathy (prostatic hypertrophy); mechanical gastrointestinal obstruction, paralytic ileus, severe ulcerative colitis/toxic megacolon; myasthenia gravis (unless used to treat cholinergic crisis).", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 0.5 mg/mL, 0.6 mg/mL, and 1 mg/mL ampoules.", "monitoring": "Continuous ECG/heart rate, pupillary diameter, body temperature, airway secretion dryness, bladder palpation."}

name: Ciprofloxacin
description: {"atc": "J01MA02", "indications": "Complicated urinary tract infections, pyelonephritis, bacterial prostatitis, traveler's diarrhea (shigellosis, salmonellosis), intra-abdominal infections, pulmonary Pseudomonas in cystic fibrosis, anthrax prophylaxis. WHO EML Watch Group.", "mechanism": "Fluoroquinolone: bactericidal inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, preventing DNA supercoiling, transcription, and replication.", "pharmacokinetics": "Excellent oral bioavailability (70-80%); Large volume of distribution; Moderate hepatic metabolism; Elimination predominantly renal; Half-life 4 hours.", "pearls": "Oral route provides tissue levels comparable to IV administration. Chelation interaction: Polyvalent cations (calcium, iron, aluminum, magnesium antacids) reduce oral absorption by >90% (space by >=2 hours). ⚠️ Tendinitis & Tendon Rupture (especially Achilles tendon): Risk highest in elderly patients and those taking systemic corticosteroids. ⚠️ Prolongation of QT Interval: Increases risk of Torsades de Pointes. ⚠️ Neuropsychiatric Effects & Aortic Dissection warnings: Can trigger seizures, confusion, hallucinations, and peripheral neuropathy.", "contraindications": "Concurrent use of tizanidine; history of tendon disorders related to fluoroquinolone administration; pregnancy and breast-feeding (cartilage damage in animal studies).", "dosageForms": "Oral tablets: 250 mg, 500 mg, 750 mg; IV infusion: 200 mg/100 mL, 400 mg/200 mL; ophthalmic and otic drops 0.3%.", "monitoring": "ECG (QTc interval), renal function, blood glucose (dysglycemia risk in diabetics), surveillance for tendon pain or swelling."}

name: Fluticasone
description: {"atc": "R03BA05", "indications": "Maintenance anti-inflammatory treatment of persistent asthma; moderate-to-severe COPD (combined with LABA); allergic rhinitis (intranasal). WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Potent synthetic glucocorticoid: diffuses into cells, binds the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor, translocates to the nucleus, and represses transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-4, IL-5, TNF-alpha) while upregulating anti-inflammatory lipocortin-1, downregulating airway eosinophils, mast cells, and mucosal edema.", "pharmacokinetics": "Extremely low oral systemic bioavailability (<1% due to near-complete first-pass hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4); Inhaled lung fraction acts locally before hepatic clearance; Half-life 8-11 hours.", "pearls": "Cornerstone of modern asthma maintenance therapy: treats the underlying chronic mucosal inflammation rather than just smooth muscle contraction. ⚠️ Local Adverse Effects: Oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) and dysphonia/hoarseness due to laryngeal myopathy (instruct patient to use a spacer device and ALWAYS rinse mouth with water and spit after each inhalation). High long-term doses can cause systemic effects (mild hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression, reduced bone mineral density, bruising).", "contraindications": "Primary treatment of status asthmaticus or acute bronchospasm where rapid bronchodilation is needed; untreated fungal, bacterial, or tubercular infections of the respiratory tract.", "dosageForms": "Inhalation aerosol (MDI): 50, 125, 250 mcg/actuation; Dry powder inhaler (Accuhaler); nasal spray 50 mcg/actuation.", "monitoring": "Asthma Control Test (ACT), visual inspection of oral cavity for candidiasis, pediatric growth velocity."}

name: Lidocaine
description: {"atc": "N01BB02", "indications": "Local and regional infiltration anesthesia; peripheral nerve blocks; spinal and epidural anesthesia; topical mucosal anesthesia; systemic IV lidocaine infusion for perioperative analgesia; Class Ib antiarrhythmic for ventricular arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia/VF). WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Voltage-gated sodium channel blocker (Nav1.5, Nav1.7): reversibly binds the intracellular S6 segment of domain IV, blocking sodium influx and halting axonal action potential generation and propagation. Preferentially binds active/open and inactivated states (use-dependent block).", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid onset (2-5 min); Intermediate duration (60-120 min plain, extended to 240 min with epinephrine 1:200,000); Hepatic de-ethylation by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 to monoethylglycinexylidide (MEGX); Elimination half-life 1.5-2 hours; Maximum dose: 3-4.5 mg/kg plain, up to 7 mg/kg with epinephrine.", "pearls": "⚠️ Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST): Initial signs include circumoral numbness, metallic taste in mouth, tinnitus, dizziness, visual disturbances, progressing to muscle twitching, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and cardiovascular collapse (ventricular arrhythmias, asystole). Emergency antidote: 20% Lipid Emulsion (Intralipid: 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 1 min, followed by 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion). Addition of Epinephrine (adrenaline 1:200,000) causes local vasoconstriction, reducing systemic absorption, prolonging block duration, and providing a marker for accidental intravascular injection.", "contraindications": "Complete heart block, severe sinoatrial block; known allergy to amino-amides; application of epinephrine-containing solutions to end-artery anatomical areas (digits, penis, nose, ears - risk of ischemic necrosis).", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 0.5%, 1%, 2% (with and without Epinephrine 1:200,000); 4% topical solution; 5% ointment; 10% oral spray; 2.5% Lidocaine + 2.5% Prilocaine (EMLA cream).", "monitoring": "Continuous ECG during blocks, mental status check during injection, signs of LAST, blood pressure, local site assessment."}

name: Bupivacaine
description: {"atc": "N01BB01", "indications": "Spinal (subarachnoid) anesthesia for cesarean section, lower limb and pelvic surgery; epidural analgesia (labor, postoperative pain); major plexus and peripheral nerve blocks; wound infiltration. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Amino-amide local anesthetic. High-affinity blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels. Dissociates very slowly from cardiac sodium channels during diastole ('fast-in, slow-out' kinetics), conferring profound cardiotoxicity.", "pharmacokinetics": "Slow onset (10-20 min); Long duration (3-8 hours depending on route); 95% protein bound (to alpha-1-acid glycoprotein); Hepatic metabolism by CYP3A4; Elimination half-life 2.7-3.5 hours; Maximum single dose: 2 mg/kg (up to 150 mg plain, 175-200 mg with adrenaline).", "pearls": "Marked cardiotoxicity compared to lidocaine (CC/CNS ratio is low ~2.0 vs 7.0 for lidocaine): toxic doses trigger refractory ventricular arrhythmias and electromechanical dissociation before neurological warning signs appear. Binds tightly to cardiac sodium channels and interferes with mitochondrial ATP synthesis. Accidental IV injection during labor epidural is a major historical cause of maternal cardiac arrest. Treatment: Resuscitation + Immediate 20% Lipid Emulsion rescue. Hyperbaric Bupivacaine (0.5% in 8% dextrose) used for predictable gravity-guided spinal anesthesia.", "contraindications": "Intravenous regional anesthesia (Bier's block - ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED due to risk of fatal tourniquet leak); severe cardiac conduction block; localized skin infection at puncture site; hypovolemia in neuraxial anesthesia.", "dosageForms": "Injectable: 0.25% (2.5 mg/mL) and 0.5% (5 mg/mL) isobaric; 0.5% hyperbaric (heavy with 80 mg/mL glucose); with/without Epinephrine 1:200,000.", "monitoring": "Aspiration before every 3-5 mL increment; ECG monitoring; frequent blood pressure (hypotension watch in spinal anesthesia); dermatomal sensory level testing (cold/touch)."}

name: Atropine
description: {"atc": "A03BA01", "indications": "Emergency treatment of severe symptomatic bradycardia and AV nodal heart block (ACLS algorithm); antidote for organophosphate, carbamate, and nerve agent poisoning; antisialagogue (reduction of airway secretions); co-administered with anticholinesterases. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Competitive, reversible antagonist of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (M1, M2, M3, M4, M5). Blocks vagal cardiac parasympathetic tone at M2 receptors in the SA and AV nodes, increasing sinus rate and AV conduction velocity.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset IV 1-2 minutes; Duration of vagolytic effect 1-2 hours; Hepatic metabolism ~50%; Renal excretion ~30-50% unchanged; Crosses blood-brain barrier and placenta.", "pearls": "⚠️ Paradoxical bradycardia occurs with low doses (<0.5 mg IV) due to central vagal stimulation or blockade of presynaptic inhibitory M1 receptors on postganglionic parasympathetic nerves (always give >=0.5 mg in adults). High doses cause classic 'anticholinergic toxidrome': 'Blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, red as a beet, hot as a hare, dry as a bone' (mydriasis, delirium, cutaneous flushing, hyperthermia, dry mouth/skin, urinary retention). In organophosphate poisoning, titrate until pulmonary secretions are clear and bronchospasm resolves.", "contraindications": "Acute narrow-angle glaucoma; obstructive uropathy (prostatic hypertrophy); mechanical gastrointestinal obstruction, paralytic ileus, severe ulcerative colitis/toxic megacolon; myasthenia gravis (unless used to treat cholinergic crisis).", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 0.5 mg/mL, 0.6 mg/mL, and 1 mg/mL ampoules.", "monitoring": "Continuous ECG/heart rate, pupillary diameter, body temperature, airway secretion dryness, bladder palpation."}

name: Lidocaine
description: {"atc": "N01BB02", "indications": "Local and regional infiltration anesthesia; peripheral nerve blocks; spinal and epidural anesthesia; topical mucosal anesthesia; systemic IV lidocaine infusion for perioperative analgesia; Class Ib antiarrhythmic for ventricular arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia/VF). WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Voltage-gated sodium channel blocker (Nav1.5, Nav1.7): reversibly binds the intracellular S6 segment of domain IV, blocking sodium influx and halting axonal action potential generation and propagation. Preferentially binds active/open and inactivated states (use-dependent block).", "pharmacokinetics": "Rapid onset (2-5 min); Intermediate duration (60-120 min plain, extended to 240 min with epinephrine 1:200,000); Hepatic de-ethylation by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 to monoethylglycinexylidide (MEGX); Elimination half-life 1.5-2 hours; Maximum dose: 3-4.5 mg/kg plain, up to 7 mg/kg with epinephrine.", "pearls": "⚠️ Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST): Initial signs include circumoral numbness, metallic taste in mouth, tinnitus, dizziness, visual disturbances, progressing to muscle twitching, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and cardiovascular collapse (ventricular arrhythmias, asystole). Emergency antidote: 20% Lipid Emulsion (Intralipid: 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 1 min, followed by 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion). Addition of Epinephrine (adrenaline 1:200,000) causes local vasoconstriction, reducing systemic absorption, prolonging block duration, and providing a marker for accidental intravascular injection.", "contraindications": "Complete heart block, severe sinoatrial block; known allergy to amino-amides; application of epinephrine-containing solutions to end-artery anatomical areas (digits, penis, nose, ears - risk of ischemic necrosis).", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 0.5%, 1%, 2% (with and without Epinephrine 1:200,000); 4% topical solution; 5% ointment; 10% oral spray; 2.5% Lidocaine + 2.5% Prilocaine (EMLA cream).", "monitoring": "Continuous ECG during blocks, mental status check during injection, signs of LAST, blood pressure, local site assessment."}

name: Naloxone
description: {"atc": "V03AB15", "indications": "Emergency reversal of life-threatening opioid overdose (respiratory depression, coma); reversal of unwanted opioid-induced perioperative side effects; diagnostic challenge in suspected opioid coma. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Pure competitive antagonist at mu, kappa, and delta opioid receptors, with highest affinity at mu receptors. Rapidly displaces opioid agonists from receptor binding sites.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset: IV 1-2 minutes, IM/SC 2-5 minutes, Intranasal 2-3 minutes; Duration of action: 30-90 minutes (dangerously short compared to long-acting opioids!); Hepatic glucuronidation to naloxone-3-glucuronide; Elimination half-life ~60-90 minutes.", "pearls": "⚠️ Renarcotization / Relapse Danger: The elimination half-life of Naloxone (60-90 min) is significantly shorter than that of most opioids (Morphine 3-4 hrs, Methadone 24-36 hrs, SR formulations). Patients can wake up, appear fully alert, and then lapse back into fatal respiratory depression 1-2 hours later. Continuous observation for >=4-6 hours is mandatory; repeated doses or a continuous infusion may be required. Rapid high-dose reversal in opioid-dependent individuals triggers severe acute withdrawal: sympathetic storm, severe hypertension, ventricular arrhythmias, flash pulmonary edema, and extreme agitation. Titrate in small IV increments (40-80 mcg every 2 min) until respiratory rate reaches 10-12 breaths/min.", "contraindications": "Known hypersensitivity to naloxone.", "dosageForms": "Injectable: 0.4 mg/mL and 1 mg/mL ampoules; pre-filled emergency auto-injectors; intranasal spray (Narcan): 4 mg per actuation.", "monitoring": "Respiratory rate, SpO2, level of consciousness, duration of opioid clearance, signs of precipitated withdrawal."}

name: Atropine
description: {"atc": "A03BA01", "indications": "Emergency treatment of severe symptomatic bradycardia and AV nodal heart block (ACLS algorithm); antidote for organophosphate, carbamate, and nerve agent poisoning; antisialagogue (reduction of airway secretions); co-administered with anticholinesterases. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Competitive, reversible antagonist of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (M1, M2, M3, M4, M5). Blocks vagal cardiac parasympathetic tone at M2 receptors in the SA and AV nodes, increasing sinus rate and AV conduction velocity.", "pharmacokinetics": "Onset IV 1-2 minutes; Duration of vagolytic effect 1-2 hours; Hepatic metabolism ~50%; Renal excretion ~30-50% unchanged; Crosses blood-brain barrier and placenta.", "pearls": "⚠️ Paradoxical bradycardia occurs with low doses (<0.5 mg IV) due to central vagal stimulation or blockade of presynaptic inhibitory M1 receptors on postganglionic parasympathetic nerves (always give >=0.5 mg in adults). High doses cause classic 'anticholinergic toxidrome': 'Blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, red as a beet, hot as a hare, dry as a bone' (mydriasis, delirium, cutaneous flushing, hyperthermia, dry mouth/skin, urinary retention). In organophosphate poisoning, titrate until pulmonary secretions are clear and bronchospasm resolves.", "contraindications": "Acute narrow-angle glaucoma; obstructive uropathy (prostatic hypertrophy); mechanical gastrointestinal obstruction, paralytic ileus, severe ulcerative colitis/toxic megacolon; myasthenia gravis (unless used to treat cholinergic crisis).", "dosageForms": "Injectable solution: 0.5 mg/mL, 0.6 mg/mL, and 1 mg/mL ampoules.", "monitoring": "Continuous ECG/heart rate, pupillary diameter, body temperature, airway secretion dryness, bladder palpation."}

name: Nitrous oxide
description: {"atc": "N01AX63", "indications": "Adjunct to general inhalational anesthesia for maintenance of analgesia; labor analgesia (Entonox: 50% N2O / 50% O2); procedural sedation for minor trauma and dental procedures. WHO EML Essential.", "mechanism": "Non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist (analgesic effect); stimulates endogenous opioid peptide release in periaqueductal gray; weak GABA-A receptor facilitation.", "pharmacokinetics": "MAC 104% (cannot produce surgical anesthesia alone under normobaric conditions); Blood-gas partition coefficient 0.47 (rapid onset and offset); 'Second gas effect' accelerates uptake of co-administered volatile anesthetics.", "pearls": "Diffuses 34x faster into air-filled closed body cavities than nitrogen leaves them: strictly contraindicated in pneumothorax, bowel obstruction, air embolism, middle ear surgery, and post-vitrectomy retinal gas bubbles. Oxidizes cobalt in vitamin B12, irreversibly inhibiting methionine synthase (risk of megaloblastic anemia, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord with chronic abuse or MTHFR deficiency). Diffusion hypoxia at end of case requires 100% O2 for 5 minutes.", "contraindications": "Pneumothorax, decompression sickness, intestinal obstruction, recent eye surgery with intraocular gas, head injury with impaired consciousness, severe pulmonary hypertension.", "dosageForms": "Medical gas cylinder (blue cylinder, liquid-gas equilibrium at 50 bar) or premixed with oxygen (50:50 Entonox).", "monitoring": "Fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2 > 30% always to avoid hypoxic gas mixture), pulse oximetry, continuous capnography."}
